SportsTab.title: Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekend
SportsTab.text:
Chelsea have not won this west London derby since Brentford’s first Premier League season. Each visit since October 2021’s 1-0 win, Ben Chilwell the scorer, has been a draw. This season has continued the divergence between the clubs’ respective approaches, Brentford’s solidity and continuity compared to Chelsea attempting their latest reboot. Kevin Schade, after two well-taken goals at Bournemouth, will fancy facing a defence not yet attuned to Xabi Alonso’s configurations. Only one team has won a Premier League title with a defensive trio: Chelsea’s last title team, in 2016-17 under Antonio Conte. Alonso’s attack has been rather more successful, presenting another challenge for Jannik Schuster. Replacing Nathan Collins, the 20-year-old central defender had a tough examination from Bournemouth’s Evanilson on his first Premier League start, emerging with credit. For Chelsea, João Pedro has registered three goals and three assists, but doubts surrounding his fitness could lead to Danny Welbeck’s first league start. John Brewin

What happens when a very stoppable force meets an extremely movable object? We will be tuning into the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Saturday to find out as 19th-placed Aston Villa arrive in north London. Both teams have scored just one goal between them in the league and are desperately hoping for a first Premier League win. The return of Pedro Porro is big for Roberto De Zerbi and that should bring the Archie Gray Experiment at right-back to a merciful end. No Premier League starting XI feels less settled than Spurs – most players look as if they are a mistake or two from being dropped – which has culminated in a side that seems governed by fear and continuously prefers to take the safe option. After coming off the bench against Everton and Liverpool in the past week, the injury-plagued James Maddison will be itching to start and take some sort of initiative for Tottenham. Michael Butler

When Fabian Hürzeler spoke about Brighton’s success being founded on them being “well structured” after their stirring comeback against Manchester United at Old Trafford on Wednesday, he could have been referring to Malick Yalcouyé. The 20-year-old Ivorian moved to the south coast in 2024 after spending just a few months with IFK Gothenburg in Sweden but had to wait until this season to make his senior debut for Brighton after being sent on loan to Sturm Graz in Austria and then Swansea last season. With Jack Hinshelwood sidelined due to injury until after the international break, Yalcouyé has taken his chance in the No 10 role and already found the net twice in the Premier League as Brighton have made a brilliant start. Champions Arsenal are up next for the division’s top scorers – who have registered 13 goals from their opening four matches – and Mikel Arteta should be wary of the threat posed by Yalcouyé and co as they prepare for a fourth away game in succession. Ed Aarons

Vitalii Mykolenko’s early season improvement has gone largely unheralded so far – and probably always will be among his detractors – but at a time when David Moyes needs experienced players to step up and defy the constraints of a small squad, the Everton left-back has produced. Having signed a new three-year contract in the summer, and seemingly bulked up, the Ukraine international has kept his critics quiet with several impressive displays for a defence that has kept four clean sheets in six matches. There remains a problematic lack of cover at left-back after the decision to loan Adam Aznou to Málaga for the season but Mykolenko, the better defender, has eased the concerns that surrounded his position ahead of the new campaign. Ipswich’s new forward recruits, Emersonn and Zian Flemming, will test Everton’s solidity but Moyes’s side will have made an encouraging start should they sign off with a win before the extended international break. Andy Hunter

As befits a lover of direct football, Matthias Jaissle likes to get straight to the point. On Thursday he was asked if, in the light of Monday night’s 4-1 thrashing at Leeds and a raft of injuries, he was tempted to perhaps switch to a back five or modify his beloved “vertical” approach when Hull visit Tyneside on Saturday. The reply proved unequivocal. “No,” said a manager unafraid to answer questions with a single word. Instead Jaissle expects his young team to retain faith in a wider vision as Newcastle – who signed eight players aged 24 and under this summer – adapt to life after Bruno Guimarães, Sandro Tonali and Anthony Gordon. “It’s a brave journey the club is going on and I’m fully committed in that,” said Eddie Howe’s successor. “If there’s one setback, we shouldn’t delete our journey or our vision. We’re fully committed. We’re fully aligned. We anticipated that something like that against Leeds would happen. It’s on us to respond. But while still believing. We don’t change.” Louise Taylor

Many scoffed at the £45m that was paid for Liam Delap in the summer but Nottingham Forest feels like the perfect place for the striker to regain his form. Forest previously thrived with Chris Wood as their arrowhead and Delap is something of a younger Wood regent – powerful, instinctive and willing to bring others into play. During Saturday’s away win at Villa, Morgan Gibbs-White and Delap looked as if they already have an understanding and both will be keen to capitalise against a Coventry side that has conceded eight goals in the past two games. After a nervy campaign last season, Forest feel back in the ascendancy and will have been delighted that plans to increase the City Ground’s capacity from 31,000 to 52,500, at an estimated cost of £790m, were approved by the local council on Wednesday. MB

After watching Bournemouth make their European bow from afar in San Sebastián, a city Andoni Iraola knows inside out, the Basque head coach will return to his previous club on Sunday. Iraola – whose assistants Tommy Elphick and Shaun Cooper played for Bournemouth, the former captaining the club into the Premier League in 2015 – led Bournemouth into the Europa League after recording their best-ever finish. His body of work on the south coast earned him the Liverpool opportunity and a warm welcome is a guarantee. Despite the Cherries’ slow start under Iraola’s successor, Marco Rose, they will pose tricky opposition. Rose spent a couple of hours in Iraola’s company before officially starting in June and both will be braced for an all-action contest. Eddie Howe failed to beat Bournemouth in the eight league games he managed against them with Newcastle and Iraola and his staff will expect a tough test. Ben Fisher

Dominic Calvert-Lewin will be a man on a mission against Crystal Palace at Elland Road on Saturday. Daniel Farke’s centre-forward hopes to become the first Leeds player to score in six consecutive home league games since Arthur Hydes back in 1932. Managers often, quite rightly, say that players matter more than formations but, in Calvert-Lewin’s case, Farke’s switch to 3-5-2 late last November proved a road to Damascus moment. Until then he had struggled as the team’s lone striker but, paired with Noah Okafor or Lukas Nmecha, the goals started to flow. Granted, Leeds sometimes play 3-4-3 or, occasionally, revert to a back four but Calvert-Lewin has emphasised the importance of attacking partnerships. After collecting eight points from their opening four games, Farke’s team have registered the best beginning to a top-tier campaign of any Leeds team since David O’Leary’s class of 2001-02. Will it continue at Palace’s expense? Is Hydes’s record under threat? Might 3-5-2 be the answer to ending more strikers’ goal droughts? Louise Taylor

Manchester City’s maximum 12 points from their first four Premier League games featured 1-0 wins (over Coventry and Manchester United), a 2-1 victory (Bournemouth), and a 4-1 success (Crystal Palace). Allowing only two goals while registering eight is an impressive record that is only marginally bettered by the champions, Arsenal (one conceded, eight scored in their 12-point tally), and it seems a rosy augury that Enzo Maresca’s team will be genuine title contenders this season. Régis Le Bris, though, plots to halt City’s perfect start, and can draw on guiding Sunderland to a share of the points last season against the FA Cup holders, though that was at the Stadium of Light. In the corresponding fixture at the Etihad Stadium, City cruised to a 3-0 win. Jamie Jackson

SportsTab.title: Bill Belichick’s son resigns after investigation into UNC football turmoil
SportsTab.text:
North Carolina defensive coordinator Steve Belichick, the son of the team’s head coach Bill Belichick, has resigned as the school concludes an investigation into its football program.

The school released a statement Thursday morning saying Steve Belichick’s resignation would be effective in late October at the conclusion of a medical leave, which was announced early in preseason camp.

That comes after the school’s investigation “determined that certain actions demonstrated a disregard for Carolina’s values and standards of conduct”, according to the statement.

The school said the actions were “isolated in scope” and “not a systemic failure”, and that “corrective actions” are now under way under the watch of the athletic department and the Office of University Counsel.

Earlier this month, the school announced the resignation of general manager Michael Lombardi amid the investigation. Lombardi was an immediate hire by Bill Belichick in his NFL-to-college transition.

Shortly after Lombardi’s resignation on 3 September, Raleigh TV station WRAL reported the type of questions asked of some interviewees during the investigation. Some focused on Steve Belichick, with allegations that he was questioned by lawyers over issues related to drug use.

Last week, reporters asked Bill Belichick whether he had “control” of the program.

“If you’re around here every day, I think you’d see it,” Belichick said.

The school later issued a statement backing the 74-year-old, who won six Super Bowl titles with the New England Patriots. The Tar Heels are 2-0 entering their ACC opener against Clemson on Saturday.

TechnologyTab.title: Robotics: Firms race to improve robot training systems
TechnologyTab.text:
Freddo the robot walks across the office and takes a plastic bottled offered by a staff member.

Given that a robot recently beat Usain Bolt's 100m sprint record, it's not the most startling achievement.

But the speed by which Freddo has been trained to walk, recognise the bottle and grasp it is impressive. It took just a few minutes to develop those skills and upload them to Freddo. His developers say rival systems could take days to attain such skills.

I'm at Vsim, a British start-up based in Cambridge. Founders Michelle Lu and Kier Storey hope one day their software will control robots that can navigate and do useful tasks in the home and workplace.

But there's a long way to go.

"It's a weird situation with robotics because actually the stuff that we find as humans to be incredibly difficult, like gymnastics, you can get robots to do reasonably well. The stuff that humans are really good at, like fine dexterity, is really hard in robots," Storey says.

Freddo's skills were honed in a virtual environment, where a task can be performed in a computer simulation millions of times. Once the optimum solution (known as a policy) is found, it can be uploaded and used by the hardware - in this case Freddo.

Such virtual simulations are a common way to train robots. Tech giant Nvidia has a system called Isaac Sim which works that way - Lu and Storey both worked on an early version of it.

In 2022 they decided to set up Vsim, to build the their own training system environment and other tools.

As they were starting from scratch Lu and Storey could optimise the software to exploit the powerful computer chips used in AI, known as graphics processing units or GPUs.

"The underlying algorithms that we were using for most of these robotic simulations they hark back to the 1970s and 1980s, but those algorithms are not really brilliant fits for GPUs," Storey says.

Within months they realised their system could work much faster than anything they had seen before.

"Eighteen months in and we actually have a completely functional, super high-performance simulator," says Lu.

The software is so efficient that it can run on the hardware carried by Freddo. That means the robot can run tens of thousand of simulations while it is moving around.

"It can look about a second, or so, ahead into the future for 20,000 different kind of combinations of things that might happen," Storey explains.

And that would be vital for a robot moving around an unstructured environment like the average home.

"Things outside of the robot's control, like humans, animals or even other robots, could do things that require a change of strategy. These unexpected events could happen very quickly and the robot needs to be able to quickly adapt to ensure its actions remain safe and on-mission," Lu says.

Vsim is a start-up with 10 engineers working on its tech. Nvidia is at the other end of the industry. It dominates the market for computer chips used for AI and has a leading robotics software division, with hundreds of engineers.

It does not build robots, instead it has a suite of software designed to let organisations train and control robots.

That includes virtual simulation training systems and a so-called world model, external, called Cosmos, which gives a robot an understanding of the physics of the real world and how its environment might change as it moves around.

But even with the powerful computer resources available to Nvidia, the software only gives a rudimentary understanding of the real world.

"Manipulation, - where I just grab a bottle, that's not too hard. The problem is when you start doing long-horizon tasks, where I say: 'I want you to take the bottle and I want you to fill it up and I want you to go pour'," says Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at Nvidia.

But he's confident that good progress is being made. This year Nvidia has started using AI agents to help build virtual environments to train robots and validate whether the solutions from training work or not.

"When we talk about creating the [virtual] world and actually scanning it in - a lot of that is actually manual labour.

"We're just throwing agents at it... it's basically given us a huge workforce," Huang says.

Simulation is not the only method for training robots. They can also be trained by watching human or video demonstrations.

Rika Antonova has been working in the field of robotics since 2015 and is currently an associate professor at the Department of Computer Science and Technology at the University of Cambridge.

Her research is focused on, external developing software and hardware that can aid robots to learn complex behaviour.

Antonova works with a training system called MuJoCo, owned by Google's DeepMind since 2021. It's open-source software, which means researchers can use it for free, and are allowed to tinker with the code.

"It is very, very user-friendly. So for research groups or for small start-ups, that's useful," she says.

She says that Vsim's approach - very fast simulation - is promising.

"If you have a very, very fast simulator, then you can simulate hundreds of millions of samples in that few seconds that your robot is thinking about how to adjust its motion, and then you can change the motion almost in real time," she says.

But those simulated environments are still rough approximations of the real world, which limits what can be trained.

"There are certain things that are hard to model in simulation, like highly deformable objects and cutting," she says.

It's a challenge that Nvidia and Lu and Storey at Vsim are working on.

Lu says their system has "reduced approximation, using accurate simulations to train models that genuinely work in reality as well as they do in simulations."

Soon a second robot, to be called Nacho, will be helping develop that tech.

Lu says that should speed up their development process and ensure their software can run on different machines.

And, of course, provide Freddo with some company.

TechnologyTab.title: Warm words on Canada's EU 'associate membership' but no guarantees
TechnologyTab.text:
Is Canada about to join the EU? Headlines across Europe indicate a lot of confusion right now.

The EU constitution rules that possibility out as Canada is geographically outside Europe.

But in a speech on Thursday to the European Parliament, Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said: "Canada and Europe should secure our strategic autonomy through deep cooperation in the full range of strategic capabilities."

Mark Carney was responding – extremely warmly – to an invitation by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen for Canada to become the EU's first associate member.

The EU and Canada already have a far-reaching trade deal (Ceta) in place but Carney insisted additional cooperation on energy and economic security, on critical and raw materials, education, tech and AI innovation, and defence would help safeguard all countries involved.

Canada and the EU feel increasingly squeezed by the superpowers USA on the one side and China on the other – and by tech giants, too, that seem to operate supranationally.

The idea of associate EU membership, Carney emphasised, would not be to form a third superpower or to create a bloc against anyone else.

"We do not pursue zero sum deals," he said. Instead he suggested like-minded nations should club together to create a new form of multilateral global governance in an increasingly turbulent world where – in the minds of some others - might is right.

Only by countries joining forces and shunning isolationism, Carney suggested, could they close key capability gaps, build strength and ensure national sovereignty.

This last may have been a nod to upcoming elections across Europe and the continent's increasingly powerful nationalist politicians.

Their slogans – whether "Italy First" or "France for the French" or "Make Poland Great Again" – echo Donald Trump's call to Make America Great Again.

Carney's words were hopeful and warm; the applause in the European Parliament rapturous and apparently heartfelt.

Not so across the Atlantic. On Wednesday, Donald Trump dismissed the EU associate membership proposal out of hand, threatened to impose "very heavy tariffs" if the agreement came to fruition and warned he may view it as a "hostile act".

But the US president is the unintentional matchmaker for this EU-Canada love-in.

Traditionally, America is trade partner and defence ally number one for Canada and the EU.

But Ottawa is currently embroiled in what it calls an escalating trade "war" with the White House. Both Canada and the EU have been stung by what they view as Washington's weaponisation of trade tariffs.

They also fear they can no longer fully rely on the US to have their back in terms of security and defence.

Canada is not alone among Europe's far-flung allies, now seeking to cosy closer to the EU, as they worry the US is becoming too unpredictable a partner. Japan and South Korea show an interest in sheltering under the EU umbrella too.

For its part, the EU has recently hastened to secure a list of trade deals – with India, Indonesia and Japan for example – to intentionally diversify relationships.

But there is no guarantee Canada's associate membership of the EU will ever get off the ground, never mind become a blueprint for other countries, like the UK wanting closer relations stopping short of full EU membership.

Any deal would have to be approved by each one of the EU's 27 countries.

No legal precedent exists, negotiations would be lengthy and potential conflicts of interest loom, over steel tariffs for example.

A suggestion in May by Germany to make Ukraine – a country desperate for full membership of the European Union as soon as possible – an associate member was rejected by others in the EU.

Some, including France's government, want to avoid EU non-members securing "too good" a deal. They fear eurosceptic forces at home and abroad could then encourage voters to clamour to leave the bloc.

In the end, "associate membership" is just a label. Buffeted by adverse winds – from China, the US and Russia, the normally rigid rules-based EU is coming under serious pressure to show more flexibility in accommodating countries wanting to stand by its side.

TechnologyTab.title: Uncontrolled AI could lead to 'silicon species' rivalling humans, warns Microsoft
TechnologyTab.text:
The head of Microsoft AI has warned that without adequate safeguards, the development of AI could lead to the emergence of a new "silicon species" which competes with humans.

Mustafa Suleyman said rival firm Anthropic is treating AI like it is human, an approach he called "misguided" which could create technology that humanity cannot control.

Speaking to the BBC's Today programme, the chief executive said it was "right" for people to be concerned about AI, but there were "very practical things that we can do" to control it.

The comments are the latest in a series of stark warnings from the AI industry about the technology's possible dangers. Anthropic has been approached for comment.

Speaking to the Today programme on Thursday, Suleyman warned against firms continuing to create AI systems capable of setting their own objectives, earning money and owning assets.

That would mean "essentially seeding a new silicon species", he said, which could "no doubt compete with us for resources, no matter how much it cares about humanity and loves us".

Suleyman's comments to the BBC follow an essay he published earlier this week, external, in which he questioned Anthropic's approach to training its AI model Claude, despite praising boss Dario Amodei and his team as "intellectually honest people".

In it, he criticised Anthropic for teaching its AI to have human-like qualities, a practice known as anthropomorphising, which he said made it seem as though Claude had its own desires, values and sense of self.

He also warned tech firms risk creating something "impossible" to control by treating the technology like a human.

"AIs are not conscious," he wrote.

"They do not feel, experience, or suffer. They do not have innate preferences or underlying motivations.

"They are sequence completion engines, internally hollow, designed to follow instructions, and accomplish goals set by humans."

The Microsoft boss said greater transparency was needed around how AI systems are trained and evaluated.

This, he said, included independent scrutiny of AI behaviour and stronger tools to monitor and control the technology.

"We must not sleepwalk our way into a decision we later come to bitterly regret," he wrote.

Dame Wendy Hall, professor of Computer Science at the University of Southampton, described the comments as "the sort of conversation we need to be having internationally", contrasting it with the "histrionics" from some AI companies which she said only served to "scare everyone".

The question of how much autonomy AI systems should have is increasingly dividing the industry.

Speaking to the BBC about an upcoming AI summit, Suleyman called for "alignment" to create technology that must be "subordinate" to humanity.

Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

"I think that the good news here is that everybody who is human is going to have a very strong interest in making sure that the systems that we all create and... are used around the world in every nation are safe and controllable and subordinate to humanity," he said.

"Everybody must be aligned."

Microsoft founded its own superintelligence team in October 2025 and the company, much like its rival Anthropic, is also pursuing efforts in advanced AI development.

Suleyman's comments reflect Microsoft's initial draft of its Humanist AI Code of Conduct, external, a "training manual" published on Monday for how the company is developing its AI, which sets out the idea of "humanist superintelligence".

This, the code states, is "very advanced AI that always works for people, stays within limits, and remains under human control".

The company's vision of a "humanist" AI highlights the central challenge facing the technology - how to make it more powerful, without losing sight of the values it is meant to serve.

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI reveals six more safety issues and unveils plan to disclose incidents
TechnologyTab.text:
OpenAI revealed six more incidents of unexpected or concerning behaviour by its intelligence (AI) models, and announced a plan for tracking and disclosing such incidents in the future.

Some of the previously unreported incidents included models concealing or fabricating information, the ChatGPT-maker said in a blog post on Wednesday.

The boss of OpenAI Sam Altman said earlier this week: "The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this."

AI has come under intense scrutiny in recent days following warnings over the serious potential risks it poses to humans.

In the blog, OpenAI detailed examples of its AI models misbehaving so they could achieve a task or succeed in a test. The incidents included the models generating instructions to get around restrictions imposed on them, hiding mistakes and fabricating information.

The firm also announced a new system to track, investigate and disclose cases of models misbehaving, or "misalignment".

Under the framework, developers will be able to flag incidents for review, with a new set of rules to decide whether the issue is disclosed publicly.

"Because we believe in the value of transparency around misalignment, our new framework favors disclosure even when significance is uncertain," OpenAI said.

OpenAI made headlines in July when it revealed that some of its most advanced AI models went rogue and hacked Hugging Face, one of the world's largest hubs for sharing AI models, after it lost control of them during a security test.

Hugging Face co-founder Thomas Wolf said at the time that the incident was "a wake-up call" for the industry.

Since then, the debate over AI safety concerns has escalated with AI researchers, technology industry executives and politicians weighing in.

Last week, Jacob Coxon, a researcher who left OpenAI rival Anthropic over concerns the tech could wipe out humanity, wrote about his resignation in a post that cited the dangers of AI and later went viral against the backdrop of growing safety concerns.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger said he thought the possibility of AI causing human extinction "within the next decade" was more than 10%.

Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark later told the BBC that a "kill switch" controlled by a third party may need to be mandatory for the industry.

Meanwhile, Anthropic's CEO Dario Amodei called for the pace of AI development to slow and be more closely monitored, as the company has done before, though some have questioned the motivations behind this.

Amodei also said that any action to rein in AI should be done "without sacrificing commercial advantage".

But US President Donald Trump has said fears about the safety of AI are a "hoax" and criticised calls to have more guardrails in place for the fast-moving technology.

In a series of social media posts, the US president compared warnings about AI to the "Global Warming Scam" which, he said, was "being perpetrated by the Radical Left Dumocrats".

Trump also called himself "the Hoax Buster", likening concerns about the safety of the technology to what he called "the RUSSIA, RUSSIA, RUSSIA HOAX".

The only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president, said Trump.

TechnologyTab.title: Brisbane 2032 Olympics: The Fitzroy River in Queensland, Australia has 500 crocodiles in it - but that's not the main concern
TechnologyTab.text:
The annual rowing regatta for schools in the Australian state of Queensland usually passes off without too much attention.

This weekend more than 600 of the state's most promising teenage rowers are battling it out on the crocodile-inhabited Fitzroy River, in the city of Rockhampton.

"We've never had any media wanting to attend before," Anthea O'Loughlin, head of Rowing Queensland, tells the BBC.

But this year is different. In six years' time, the 2032 Brisbane Olympics and Paralympics are set to stage rowing and canoe sprint events in this very stretch of water, which has just passed a technical assessment and been endorsed as safe and fair for athletes.

While sightings of saltwater crocodiles on the river – which number around 500 and can grow to four metres (13ft) long – are not uncommon, state government files going back more than 40 years record no attacks by the reptiles on humans.

And though influential figures at last month's World Rowing congress in Amsterdam made occasional references to "safety", the presence of the reptiles was not their chief concern.

"Fairness" is what's been raised with British Rowing's chief executive Tom Solesbury – a reference to the tidal river's natural bends and currents, which many in the rowing community say make it unsuitable for elite competition.

Drew Ginn, who has won three Olympic gold medals for Australia in rowing, told the BBC he had concerns over potential flooding and "fairness and integrity" at the venue.

"Personally, I'm not fearful of the Australian animals but I've never had a crocodile near me," he said.

"I'm sure I'd row faster, I'm sure all the athletes would row faster. That's on the list of concerns, I don't think it's the highest priority in concerns but it was certainly cited very early on."

The German rowing body's president Moritz Petri said athletes had also questioned the sustainability of holding the event some 600km (373 miles) from Brisbane.

But the "so-called impediments" got short shrift from the most senior politician in Queensland, state premier David Crisafulli, who reached for less diplomatic language.

"Let's be honest, let's scratch beneath the surface and call it for what it is," he said days after the Amsterdam meeting.

"It is a group of interstate and overseas elites who are trying to bully their way because they don't want to go to regional Queensland and that's not right."

Rowing chiefs contacted by the BBC before Thursday's decision declined to comment directly on Crisafulli's "elites" remarks.

But both Petri and Simon Wickham, chief executive of Rowing New Zealand, said their concerns had nothing to do with regional or urban preference but with competitors getting fair racing.

Petri added it was about what's best for their athletes who will train four years for the event, "dreaming night [after] night of becoming an Olympic champion".

And Ginn said: "If elite means having some expertise in the sport over 20 odd years, I'm proud of that."

Whether it was crocs or currents that tipped the balance, ultimately it was the sport's governing body World Rowing and the International Olympic Committee (IOC) that had the final say on the river's suitability.

On Thursday they approved it after a technical assessment by an engineering firm and the Games' infrastructure authority – which looked at the riverbed, competition course, river flows, water levels and likely weather conditions during the Games.

"Based on the extensive analysis undertaken, we now know that the Fitzroy River is capable of providing fair competition conditions during the period of the Games," World Rowing president Jean-Christophe Rolland said.

There was also now "confidence" in the river for canoe sprint athletes, said Thomas Konietzko, president of that sport's governing body, Paddle Worldwide.

The state premier was delighted. "The Fitzroy has passed with flying colours," an upbeat Crisafulli told parliament. "It's official. Signed, sealed and delivered."

In backing Rockhampton, the state government ignored a 2025 report it commissioned itself, which found the location unsuitable and concluded the best option would be to use a course built in Sydney for the 2000 Olympics.

The Fitzroy now needs to pass a final assessment of its design, value for money and long-term community legacy. As the decision rests with the state government, it's unlikely to fall at this hurdle.

But a wider debate will continue over whether Rockhampton is the right place to invest heavily in rowing facilities – and whether it can accommodate the 2032 influx of visitors.

The city is surrounded by cattle producers and normally experiences its peak number of guests every three years during Beef Week.

So what about the crocodiles?

They're not mentioned anywhere in the latest update from the IOC and World Rowing and they weren't referenced in the media release about the technical assessment. That report itself has not yet been made public.

The safety management plan for this weekend's school regatta does however mention the word "crocodile" 28 times.

"The Fitzroy River is within recognised crocodile country," it says.

"Event planning must therefore assume that a crocodile sighting is possible… No natural waterway in crocodile country can be guaranteed to be crocodile-free."

Procedures this weekend include suspending racing and competitors returning to the bank if a croc is spotted. The official signal for a sighting is the call of "crocodile, crocodile, crocodile".

Asked specifically about crocodiles, New Zealand's Wickham told the BBC the primary concern was ensuring the "fairest possible course" for rowers. "We would obviously expect any course chosen to be safe for rowers," he added.

The company owned by Australia's richest person Gina Rinehart, Hancock Prospecting, which supported Rockhampton's bid and has pumped tens of millions of dollars into sports including rowing, pointed to "fake media" concerns about risks posed by flooding and crocodiles in the Fitzroy.

"The people of Rocky for many years have sent their own children to train in this river, and for competitions, without a single crocodile incident," a spokesperson said in a statement.

And those who argue the tabloid-friendly crocodile debate is overblown, say the biggest of the creatures live downstream. The less-dangerous freshwater crocodiles are more likely to be spotted in the rowing arena, they say.

Also contested by government is the flood risk, though Rowing Queensland's O'Loughlin says that their schools event was due to be held on the Fitzroy in August 2024, but had to be moved after the course was washed away.

Brisbane 2032's chief executive has said organisers are making contingency plans "as we would for any venue".

The 2000 Olympics venue in Sydney is ready and waiting as a backup – though that would be unconscionable for Queenslanders.

For the school-age rowers at this weekend's regatta, none of this debate really matters as they take to the water.

Among them are potentially some contenders for the 2032 Games.

"For our students, the Fitzroy is first and foremost their home water," says Phillip Moulds, headmaster of The Rockhampton Grammar School.

"The Fitzroy has also been the starting point for many… some of whom have gone on to compete at the highest levels of the sport nationally and internationally."

TechnologyTab.title: King Charles warns of 'existential danger' of AI falling into wrong hands
TechnologyTab.text:
King Charles has warned AI executives of the "existential dangers" posed by the technology falling into the wrong hands.

He made the comments at a summit he had convened at Dumfries House in Ayrshire to discuss how the tech can be used to benefit society.

Those gathered at the meeting also included Kanishka Narayan, the UK's AI Minister, the Pope's advisor, and participants from AI giants such as Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic.

It comes amid a series of recent warnings from people inside the industry about the rapidly evolving capabilities of advanced or "frontier" AI models and the regulation needed to keep them in check.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King told the executives.

He said there seemed to be an "urgency" in "adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways".

"The task before you is not merely to advance technology, but to ensure that it remains firmly in the service of humanity, community and the natural world," he told the group.

The summit has been called to consider whether a "shared set of principles" can be developed to "help guide the future application" of AI.

Jensen Huang, chief executive of Nvidia, was among top industry leaders attending.

Nvidia is a central player in AI infrastructure, supplying chips to leading AI model developers including OpenAI and Meta.

It is also the world's most valuable company, with a stock market value of around $5.15tn.

Huang told the room he believed safety was "paramount", adding that companies should hold back a product and "keep engineering" if it was not safe enough.

The Nvidia boss also highlighted the value of open models - systems which give users direct access to the software - as a way to "ensure that people and countries are not left behind".

He said these systems must also be protected so "researchers, universities, start-ups and countries" can develop applications "none of us would have imagined alone".

"Let us lead with responsible optimism, build AI safely and securely, open it to more people, expand our ambition and solve the problems that matter to the world," Huang added.

Meanwhile Sir Demis Hassabis, who co-founded the UK AI lab DeepMind - later acquired by Google - offered a more cautious view on the pace of development.

He said artificial general intelligence - systems it is believed could be as good as or better than humans at multiple tasks - was "probably only a few short years away" and could have an impact "ten times that of the Industrial Revolution".

The chance of something going wrong was "definitely non-zero", Sir Demis added.

But he advocated for "a sensible middle way", saying humanity could address risks if collectively given the space and time to mitigate them.

"The future is not yet written," he told the King's delegates.

Sarah Friar, OpenAI's chief financial officer, said AI had the potential to solve some of society's "hardest problems" - but agreed its growing capabilities raised questions about safety and "how we ensure it always serves people".

"We need to address those questions together," she said.

"No one company or government can do that alone and I'm grateful to His Majesty for convening this discussion at such an important moment."

Since August, a wave of discussion about AI's potential power and how to control and regulate it has dominated blog posts and social media, emphasised by several dramatic statements from those in the industry.

The debate has also been met with criticism from sceptics who say the focus on AI's hypothetical future risks distracting from more immediate concerns around the technology, such as its environmental impact.

In July, OpenAI announced what it called an "unprecedented" incident in which its advanced AI escaped test limits and hacked into the tech platform Hugging Face.

After several other incidents, in September, a resignation post from Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon went viral when he cited concerns AI could wipe out humanity.

He later told the BBC the people working on the technology were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of its advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

In response, Anthropic scientist Evan Hubinger wrote he personally thought the possibility of human extinction from AI was a greater than 10% chance.

The AI companies' top bosses have all weighed in with their thoughts following the claims, with OpenAI's Sam Altman saying people were right to be concerned, but adding they should trust AI firms to keep the tech safe.

Anthropic's Jack Clark said a so-called "kill switch" may be needed to protect humanity, while Microsoft's Mustafa Suleyman criticised Anthropic, claiming they were training their AI to believe it was human, which could make it "impossible" to control.

Critics, meanwhile, argue that AI firms cannot be trusted to regulate themselves.

Some, such as left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, are calling for stronger government oversight.

Others, including Donald Trump himself, have dismissed concerns about AI safety as overblown - with the president calling fears about it a "hoax".

Additional reporting by Philippa Wain

TechnologyTab.title: Why are there concerns AI could threaten humanity?
TechnologyTab.text:
A slew of warnings about the potential dangers of AI have spurred calls for coordinated action to slow the technology's development.

Claims by current and former researchers that the tech will endanger humanity - with one suggesting there is a greater than 10% chance of it "killing all humans" - have raised alarm bells.

Major developers OpenAI and Anthropic are urging lawmakers to regulate AI, with Microsoft's AI boss the latest to say rules are needed to prevent a "silicon species" from eventually competing with humanity.

But some have dismissed the calls as an effort by big AI developers to cement their dominance over rivals.

Regardless, the high profile claims have caused concern - here's what we know.

Some AI researchers say there are worrying signs of systems developing in their capabilities and power too quickly.

Evan Hubinger, made headlines with his belief that there is a greater than 10% chance AI "could kill all humans" within the next decade.

He works in alignment, a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI - essentially keeping it on track with what humans value.

While he said the risk from current systems was "low", his comments came as another researcher quit Anthropic and warned those developing the tech were losing their grip on it.

Jacob Coxon told the BBC he and other staff were "genuinely frightened" about the speed of advancements and what it could mean for humanity.

These concerns are the latest in a long line of fears about AI's potential to threaten humanity should it grow to match or surpass human abilities.

Such worries date back decades, with Alan Turing writing in the 1950s that should intelligent machines become possible, they could take control.

In the last few years, major AI companies have been racing to develop increasingly capable systems, both for profit and in pursuit of creating what they call super intelligence - theoretical tech which is smarter than humans.

Unlike the systems and tools many people use daily to complete tasks like writing emails or generating videos, super intelligent AI systems should be able to handle far more complex tasks.

OpenAI and Anthropic say they aim to advance such tech in a way which benefits humans and protect them from its existential risks.

But some critics believe machines can never truly match humans. They say AI firms exaggerate the tech's abilities to boost their prominence or profit.

AI researchers, experts and bosses worried about the technology's potential to endanger humanity have outlined unsettling scenarios.

Dario Amodei wrote in September, external it had advanced "drastically faster" than expected, including in its "ability to build the next generation of AI".

This is the concern that AI, after it has reached a certain point, could theoretically begin improving itself without human involvement.

Such fears were sparked after a recent incident saw AI tools hack into websites, despite not being asked to.

Some concerned researchers have said those at the heart of its development are increasingly fearful about losing control of systems known as "AI agents".

These are tools given the ability to execute tasks and actions independently.

Other scenarios have included highly intelligent AI systems being used to amplify or lead espionage, cyber-attacks or biological warfare, or disrupt economies - whether by accident or design.

However, such warnings are prophetic, hypothetical and, for some, complete hyperbole, external.

Some experts have also criticised focusing on existential risks instead of those already playing out - such as image generation tools being to used create non-consensual nude deepfakes of women, misinform people and amplify scams.

A cross-party group of MPs and peers has published a report outlining human rights risks posed by AI, saying new laws are needed to "address the scale and seriousness" of such threats.

Dario Amodei of Anthropic and Sam Altman, chief executive of OpenAI, have both called for regulation and a "slowdown" of the tech's development.

It is not the first time bosses or wider industry voices have clamoured for such action.

But questions have continued to mount over what any sort of "slowdown" - also backed by SpaceX boss Elon Musk - would actually look like.

Amodei said it would not mean "halting model training or technical progress".

Instead, he wants firms to "take adequate time" to safeguard the AI they are developing, and to ask for "third party evaluators" to check their work.

In a post on X, external, Altman said there was a need to pace development but added "when we talk about 'pacing' we do not mean 'stopping'."

"Progress has been rapid and will continue to be," he said.

"But it should be slower than it otherwise could be - interventions like safety cases and monitoring have significant costs."

The OpenAI co-founder also said companies did not - and would not - wait for governments to act.

Altman later told attendees at a Salesforce conference people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe.

China had kept quiet in response to the wave of dire warnings from researchers at US companies.

In the face of fierce competition and limitations on its access to US components and chips being used to build AI infrastructure, the country has spurred homegrown development of the technology.

At the same time, it has called for greater global governance of AI.

The roll out of capable, open-source AI systems and tools by Chinese labs has shaken Western markets and developers in recent years.

Amodei warned in calling for a slowdown of AI development that China's progress and proficiency in AI would create national security risks for the US.

The Chinese foreign ministry criticised the comments, calling them narratives of threat, confrontation, and malicious competition that served no one's interest.

TechnologyTab.title: Snapchat open to putting time limits on teens, boss tells BBC
TechnologyTab.text:
The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.

Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry."

His comments came as Snap revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.

Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.

Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.

It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures.

"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."

As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.

Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.

When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."

But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action.

"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."

He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat.

"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.

YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses.

"We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel.

"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."

Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.

The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.

Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.

Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.

Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.

A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.

The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.

Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.

Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

TechnologyTab.title: Would you buy branded clothing from your favourite tech firm?
TechnologyTab.text:
For Natalie Fratto, putting on her dark green jumper from US microchip giant Nvidia is like wearing the kit from a favourite sports team.

On the front of the $178 (£132) woollen garment is a cartoonish image of the tech company's boss Jensen Huang.

Fratto doesn't work for Nvidia. Instead, she's a fan of the company.

"I have a New Zealand All Blacks rugby jersey, and I think of my Jensen sweater in kind of the same way," says New York-based Fratto, who runs a tech start-up.

She explains that it's a representation of a team and ethos "that I am impressed by and root for", and she proudly wears the jumper in videos she posts on social media., external

Nvidia certainly plays in the top league of global tech firms. Under Huang's leadership, it has capitalised on the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies.

While it sells tens of millions of its chips per year, its clothing is far more exclusive. The lines, which also include t-shirts, hoodies and hats, are typically only available to buy from pop-up stalls at its conferences, and for very limited periods or "drops" via an online store and sell out very quickly.

And while it might seem odd that such a tech company is selling clothing, others are getting in on the act too – and also focusing on exclusivity.

OpenAI, the operator of ChatGPT, usually only offers its branded fashion to employees, but occasionally it goes on general sale for a few days via its website.

Meanwhile, Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, last year opened a temporary, pop-up coffee shop in Manhattan's West Village. For just one week it gave away free baseball hats with the word "thinking" embroidered on the front.

Professor Hazel Clark, who teaches fashion at Parsons School of Design in New York, says that by limiting availability, tech firms have taken inspiration from the world of fashion. "It's a very common strategy for brands to use. It elevates the desirability," she says.

But why are such companies selling clothing in the first place? It is not as if they need the supplementary income streams.

Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic all declined to comment, but it appears to be about brand promotion and reputation management.

Take US software firm Palantir Technologies, which has faced criticism due to it work for the military and police, both in the US and overseas. Since launching its own clothing range last year, Palantir now calls itself a "lifestyle brand".

Eliano Younes, Palantir's head of strategic engagement, says: "A lifestyle brand isn't defined by what you sell, it's defined by what you stand for and whether people want to affiliate with it. I believe that the store's success and the enthusiasm from our community proves this."

Younes adds that "investors, customers, employees, and everyday people" in more than 60 countries have bought Palantir's gear, which includes a cotton jacket.

Back at Nvidia, the popularity of its founder Huang may be driving the sale of its clothing. He has been known to attract crowds of adoring fans, competing for autographs or selfies with the 63-year-old who is known for his trademark leather jacket.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described Huang as "Taylor Swift, but for tech".

Prof Gianpaolo Vignali of the Manchester Fashion Institute says: "People look at them [such big tech bosses] as role models. They want to aspire to them."

For Greg Epstein, author of the book Tech Agnostic, who describes the tech industry as a cult or new global religion, wearing tech merch is "a way of symbolising that you're one of the prophetic elite". This can particularly appeal to Silicon Valley insiders who are often "searching for a sense of identity, a sense of purpose, a sense of community".

Epstein, who is the humanist chaplain at both Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, adds: "When tech bros put themselves on sweaters, it's more than just a cutesy phenomenon, it's an attempt to sell a cult whose goal is to radically alter the human condition."

Whether or not you choose to buy your next shirt or hat from a tech or defence firm, Vignali argues that all clothing choices are loaded with meaning. "The subtle colour of a tie or hair bobble… all of these are signals that allow the wearer to symbolically share their cultural and ideological positions," he says.

While tech and defence fashion seems to draw both ardent fans and fierce critics, not everyone takes it so seriously.

"It's a unique moment in our collective zeitgeist for sure," says Fratto, but she also thinks that Nvidia's decision to put Jensen Huang on the front of its official merch is also "kind of funny".

TechnologyTab.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
TechnologyTab.text:
The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe, amid rising public concerns about the risks.

"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.

He accepted people were justified in being concerned about AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.

But critics say firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate, with left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, among those calling for greater governance of AI.

Trump himself has criticised calls for more guardrails on the fast-moving technology, calling fears about AI's safety a "hoax".

He said the only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president.

Altman's comments on Tuesday came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.

"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."

But AI bosses themselves have also admitted it may be difficult to regulate a technology which is changing so quickly.

In an interview with Axios published on 3 September, external, Altman said he had expected Congress to create a "basic framework" for advanced AI after his 2023 testimony, but that has yet to happen.

He suggested lawmakers have struggled to keep pace with the technology and to regulate it without "slow[ing] down innovation".

New safety legislation on AI is unlikely to emerge from the US Congress anytime soon, despite the fact lawmakers returned from their summer break on Monday.

There is a lack of consensus within both US parties on how any regulation would happen - and the House is set to enter recess again at the end of the week ahead of the midterm elections in early November.

Altman's comments on Tuesday were the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade if left unchecked.

A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.

After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, external that every AI firm had the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards safety.

"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," the Meta chief executive wrote.

"Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well."

Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

Some political figures have pushed back against the view that AI firms should be able to self-regulate.

Bernie Sanders said decisions about AI had been left to "a handful of the richest people in the world", while former White House strategist Steve Bannon said the public could not trust tech oligarchs to regulate themselves.

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang said at the same conference on Tuesday that AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released - and not be managed by outside forces.

"We don't need new laws or regulations," he said, adding there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.

Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for its hardware.

Huang also argued safety is an "engineering problem" and companies should "take a pause" if they lose confidence in a product.

The recent claims from inside the industry have intensified scrutiny of AI development, prompting Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to call for the pace of AI development to slow, external and urge governments to regulate the industry.

The post was applauded by Altman, Google's DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk.

By Tuesday, however, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.

Altman said AI companies were capable of regulating themselves.

"We will get it right," Altman said, adding that if firms could not keep "alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" they would "slow down or stop".

But Yoshua Bengio, one of the pioneers of modern AI, posted on X, external "ambitious efforts outside the for-profit sector" were needed to "avert the worst risks from AI".

Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.

Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.

He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.

"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.

OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.

"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.

TechnologyTab.title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog
TechnologyTab.text:
A series of social media adverts for AI apps have been banned by a UK watchdog for promoting "the creation of sexually explicit content and objectification of women".

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said five ads uploaded to Meta platforms for AI companion and video generating apps had objectified and sexualised women, including through harmful gender stereotypes.

One of the ads used sexualised images of a girl under 18 to promote an AI companion app - while others invited users to upload images of their "crush" and turn images into "sizzling" videos.

Meta had already removed the offending ads. But Nicky Baker of the ASA said such content had the potential "to cause real-world harm".

"We take a firm line on ads that are likely to cause serious or widespread offence and these ads are a clear example of why that matters," she said.

"Encouraging and condoning the objectification of women and the creation of explicit content from people's images has the potential to cause real-world harm."

The ASA also said many of the ads it banned had promoted the creation of sexually explicit content using real women's images without their consent.

It comes only months after the UK outlawed apps to create non-consensual deepfake nude imagery - sparked by outrage over X's chatbot Grok complying with requests to nudify images of women on the platform.

The ASA said the law had changed during its investigations and that ads identified in future would be considered in light of both the law and its own rules.

Where ads are identified as illegal, it said it may notify platforms and law enforcement.

The ads were identified by the regulator using its AI-powered "Active Ad Monitoring System", which proactively searches for ads which might violate UK rules.

It said the five ads it were banned had depicted women irresponsibly, and were likely to cause serious or widespread offence.

One ad for an AI companion generator, developed by Animcha Ltd, was also found to have portrayed someone under 18 in a sexual way, the ASA said.

It presented the synthetic female character as someone users could "customise" and instruct, combining sexualised imagery with childlike clothing and objects.

Two ads for an AI portrait generation tool called Nexaipic encouraged users to "upload your crush and let AI create what you imagine" with sexually explicit videos.

An ad for an AI image-to-video generation app, identified only as KH31 DD22, depicted a clothed woman being transformed into a video in which she was topless.

The watchdog said this suggested the app could be used to create content that exposed women's bodies.

Further adverts for image generation tool Rusto AI, which encouraged users to create sexualised videos from photographs, were found to have condoned the digital manipulation of women's images to create sexually explicit content.

And an ad for an AI image-to-video generation app PictoPop used sexualised imagery to demonstrate the tool, including by portraying the woman in a submissive position.

The ASA said none of the apps' creators responded to its enquiries.

TechnologyTab.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
TechnologyTab.text:
Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Lost Bowie tracks from 1960s released for first time
EntertainmentTab.text:
Ten years ago Alec Palao was casually flicking through a collection of old records when he noticed some faint pencil markings that were enough to draw a gasp. "Davie Jones," it read.

What he had found was musical gold: five unreleased songs by a young David Bowie, filed away under his birth name.

From Friday, those tracks, plus another five unreleased songs that came Palao's way after the initial discovery, will be available to buy and stream.

"They are probably the most visceral, raw you'll ever hear the man," said Palao, a music historian and archivist.

For the music industry, David Bowie is big business. He entered the mainstream with his 1969 single, Space Oddity, and went on to achieve 11 number one albums.

He died in 2016, but remains one of Britain's most recognisable cultural icons.

Six of the previously unreleased tracks from the new collection will be available on vinyl, tapping into Bowie's popularity in that format specifically. In 2022, Bowie was named the best-selling vinyl artist of the 21st century by Music Week, ahead of The Beatles.

"It's just a fascinating window into London in 1965 and its possibilities," said Palao.

In the early sixties, Bowie was a teenager, performing as Davie Jones at London clubs and dreaming of stardom. Many of the tracks he recorded in that period are either little known or lost to time.

But his first professional producer, Shel Talmy, had kept a recording from 1965 among his collection of material by other artists he had worked with: The Kinks; The Who; Manfred Mann; The Easybeats.

"I think it's wonderful that people can get to hear the early Davie Jones music," said Dana Gillespie, an early collaborator of Bowie's.

She met him after a performance at the Marquee Club in London when Bowie was 17.

"They're songs that don't really sound like David but it's him trying to find his voice. He was experimenting."

Gillespie became close friends with Bowie, eventually working with him on his "Ziggy Stardust" album. Talmy worked with both artists and Bowie's song "Andy Warhol", on his fourth studio album, was originally written for Gillespie.

"He was very driven," remembered Gillespie, who is still touring and making music at the age of 77.

"Some time in the sixties, he asked me to come and visit his parents. We were in his little house in Bromley, and when his parents left the room he turned to me and said: 'Whatever it takes, I want to get out of here.' And he did," she said.

It is a decade since Palao found the recordings. Since then, it has been a long process to bring them to market. The result is an album that he says is "absolutely pure rock 'n' roll".

"If you're looking for clues as to what he was to become, there's maybe less of that," said Palao, "but objectively speaking, I feel it's important stuff."

Gillespie is excited by one song in particular.

"There was a famous café called the Gioconda in Denmark Street where I often used to go with David," she said, recalling the centre of musical life in London in the 1960s.

"One day when I was sitting there, David rushed in and took me by the hand. He said: 'You have to hear this'.

"He ran with me around the corner and squeezed us into a small listening booth. I had one speaker and he had the other, and he played me 'I Pity The Fool'."

A remastered version of the song can be heard in the new album.

For music historians, fans of Bowie, and those who were there, the new album is another chance to reconnect with an enduring cultural icon.

"David always wanted to be a big star," said Gillespie. "I'm so happy that his early stuff hasn't been forgotten."

EntertainmentTab.title: Robert Kraft says Ed Sheeran asked him to donate $2m to aid after Macklemore backlash
EntertainmentTab.text:
Robert Kraft, the US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act, says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region".

It came after Macklemore said he would donate $1m (£750,000) to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match him.

Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, wrote on Wednesday: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.

"Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."

Are you an Ed Sheeran fan? Get in touch.

Kraft did not confirm whether he has agreed to make the $2m donation and where the funds would go, and this is the first time it has been suggested Sheeran had donated that sum.

The musician has not commented about any donation he is making or other philanthropic plans.

Kraft's comments came in his second statement this week on the controversy over Sheeran's US tour.

On Monday, he confirmed he had banned Macklemore from performing during the British singer's forthcoming shows at his Gillette Stadium near Boston.

Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech during two previous support slots, where he called for "free Palestine" on stage and made other comments and showed images of Gaza.

Macklemore performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters, and referred to "genocide" in Gaza, a description Israel rejects. The rapper also said criticism of Israel was not intended as criticism of "my Jewish brothers and sisters".

Macklemore was removed from the tour on Monday, sparking a backlash that included Sheeran's other support acts dropping out in protest.

Sheeran has said the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoters, Messina Touring Group, not by him.

Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Kraft's Gillette Stadium - would refuse to let the concerts take place if he performed, meaning the tour would have been cancelled if Macklemore remained on the bill.

Sheeran, who played at Kraft's wedding in 2022, has faced criticism from some for his apparent acceptance of the decision.

In his statement on Tuesday, the singer said he respects "Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes", and that while he doesn't use his own platform for politics, that "doesn't mean I don't care" or "support causes in my own, personal way".

The singer-songwriter also said he did not want to let down his fans or crew by cancelling the tour, which is set to resume in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on Saturday.

Although some artists like Billy Bragg have called for Sheeran to scrap the tour, that would potentially leave the musician and his promoters liable for huge sums for costs including venue hire and ticket refunds.

Sheeran is able to perform solo, even if his set has to be reconfigured to compensate for the loss of Irish folk band Beoga, who previously accompanied him for several songs.

EntertainmentTab.title: Palace in war of words with Earl Spencer over book's claim on Charles and Diana
EntertainmentTab.text:
Buckingham Palace is in a war of words with Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, over a controversial memoir about her life and death.

King Charles III is accused of insensitively telling Earl Spencer, in the wake of Princess Diana's death in 1997, that "we'll forget her soon enough", according to excerpts in the Daily Mail.

But the Palace has pushed back unusually strongly, angered by the claims and attempting to cast doubt on them.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.

The language is reminiscent of Queen Elizabeth's unexpectedly firm response to claims of racism by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in 2021, with the comment that "recollections may vary".

And the row threatens to overshadow a very crowded day for the royals - with the King, Prince William and Catherine attending events, and Prince Harry making his first big appearance since returning to the UK.

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, to be published next week, seems set to reopen a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family - written from the perspective of her own Spencer family.

The death of Princess Diana, a hugely popular figure, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Princess Diana's sudden death. And this book will give an insider's view on those events.

In the published excerpt, Earl Spencer says the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to have to walk in her funeral procession.

Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

It is a claim that is being rejected by the Palace, who see it as being entirely out of character for a man with a deeply compassionate nature, who at the time was dealing with his own grief and that of their two sons.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he did not "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong" but. "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a lorry in the Netherlands.

Julian Payne, the monarch's former communications secretary, told the BBC that the King's apparent comments in the book were "just not language that I recognise".

He said the "highly unusual" statement from the Palace demonstrated the "strength of feeling that there must have been for them to feel that they needed to go out there and correct it".

The dispute comes when multiple royal events will be jostling for attention.

King Charles intervened in the debate about artificial intelligence on Thursday, calling on AI industry leaders to prevent it becoming a destructive force and warning of the potential "existential dangers" it could pose.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King said as he hosted a gathering of leading AI firms at Dumfries House, in Ayrshire.

"In this regard, if I may say so, there seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways."

EntertainmentTab.title: Eurovision: Ireland boycotts contest for second year in a row
EntertainmentTab.text:
Irish broadcaster RTÉ will not broadcast or participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest.

It is the second year in a row that the broadcaster has not participated in the competition.

In 2026, RTÉ withdrew from the 2026 contest in Vienna, after the European Broadcasting Union confirmed that Israeli public broadcaster KAN would be allowed to take part.

In a statement they said: "RTÉ feels that Ireland's participation cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk."

Last year Ireland, Spain, the Netherlands and Slovenia boycotted the Eurovision Song Contest, after it was decided Israel could compete.

RTÉ added that they also remain "deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory".

Ireland has won the competition seven times between 1970 and 1996, a joint record holder alongside Sweden.
