articles.title: Snapchat open to putting time limits on teens, boss tells BBC
articles.text:
The boss of Snapchat-parent Snap Inc says the firm would be "willing to implement" time limits for teens, following a call from Meta for it to take action.

Evan Spiegel told the BBC in an interview at the company's California headquarters that setting a maximum amount of time that young users could spend on the app could be "an important step forward for the industry."

His comments came as Snap revealed a slew of new features for its upcoming Specs glasses, which it said could connect to Apple iPhone and Mac devices.

Meta has been pressuring other social media companies to join it in making platform changes it agreed to as part of a recent multi-billion dollar legal settlement with US states.

Instagram and Facebook-parent Meta was facing allegations from Attorneys General for most US states who said the firm deliberately designed its apps to be addictive to young users.

It agreed to pay $12.7bn and implement a two-hour daily limit for teen users across its platforms by default, in addition to muted notifications during school hours, blocks at night and other measures.

"I think it is an important step forward in the industry in terms of really identifying industry norms, and I think that would be beneficial overall," Spiegel told the BBC. "We've looked really thoughtfully at the terms."

As part of Meta's August settlement, the company said it would implement even more stringent time limits and pay an additional $5.3bn if YouTube and TikTok follow suit. It has denied any wrongdoing as part of the deal, which will be paid over a 10-year period.

Last month, a Meta spokesperson said it was hopeful that Snap would make similar platform changes as well.

Meta, YouTube, TikTok and Snap have all faced a barrage of litigation alleging their apps have helped spawn a youth mental health crisis. Snap has also been accused of facilitating illegal drug sales.

When asked about the idea of a default time limit, Spiegel said: "I think that's a really good example of something that that we'd be willing to implement."

But Spiegel did not commit to a timeline on when Snap might take action.

"That's something we've talked about internally," he said. "I don't have more to share today."

He noted that Snap offers tools through its Family Center feature, which currently enables parents to track aspects of how their teens are using Snapchat.

"We want to figure out how we can be part of the solution," Spiegel added.

YouTube-parent Google said it had no comment when asked if it planned to implement the measures in Meta's settlement. TikTok did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

With the device, Snap aims to offer a middle ground between VR headsets like Meta's Quest 3 and lightweight AI smart glasses offered by rivals which look more like conventional glasses.

"We're creating a totally new category here," said Spiegel.

"You have a really powerful computer that brings a lot of the immersive capability you see with VR, but they're also lightweight at just about 130 grams, so they're very wearable and they have these see-through lenses, so you can use them out in the world."

Specs is Snap's most recent foray into the wearable tech, coming a decade after its short-lived Spectacles cost the company tens of millions of dollars.

The device is also arriving as Meta is facing a significant backlash over its own smart glasses, which are estimated to be the most popular of the market.

Some online derisively call them "pervert glasses" over how they have been used to secretly film women, with one person telling the BBC they were filmed leaving the beach, while another said they were told to pay to remove a video of them from the internet.

Nevertheless, sales continue to rise. With seven million pairs having been sold according to Meta.

Snap said it has built into the design of Specs, which do not use facial recognition to identify people.

A white light flashes at the top of the glasses above the users nose when it is recording video and taking a photo.

The company says that will let people nearby see that recording is happening.

Users of Meta glasses have figured out ways to obscure components meant to indicate that a photo or video is being captured, including by tampering with the electronics in the device.

Meta says it has remotely disabled the cameras on thousands of its devices on which tampering or destruction of the indicator light was detected.

articles.title: Would you buy branded clothing from your favourite tech firm?
articles.text:
For Natalie Fratto, putting on her dark green jumper from US microchip giant Nvidia is like wearing the kit from a favourite sports team.

On the front of the $178 (£132) woollen garment is a cartoonish image of the tech company's boss Jensen Huang.

Fratto doesn't work for Nvidia. Instead, she's a fan of the company.

"I have a New Zealand All Blacks rugby jersey, and I think of my Jensen sweater in kind of the same way," says New York-based Fratto, who runs a tech start-up.

She explains that it's a representation of a team and ethos "that I am impressed by and root for", and she proudly wears the jumper in videos she posts on social media., external

Nvidia certainly plays in the top league of global tech firms. Under Huang's leadership, it has capitalised on the AI boom to become one of the world's most valuable companies.

While it sells tens of millions of its chips per year, its clothing is far more exclusive. The lines, which also include t-shirts, hoodies and hats, are typically only available to buy from pop-up stalls at its conferences, and for very limited periods or "drops" via an online store and sell out very quickly.

And while it might seem odd that such a tech company is selling clothing, others are getting in on the act too – and also focusing on exclusivity.

OpenAI, the operator of ChatGPT, usually only offers its branded fashion to employees, but occasionally it goes on general sale for a few days via its website.

Meanwhile, Anthropic, the maker of the Claude chatbot, last year opened a temporary, pop-up coffee shop in Manhattan's West Village. For just one week it gave away free baseball hats with the word "thinking" embroidered on the front.

Professor Hazel Clark, who teaches fashion at Parsons School of Design in New York, says that by limiting availability, tech firms have taken inspiration from the world of fashion. "It's a very common strategy for brands to use. It elevates the desirability," she says.

But why are such companies selling clothing in the first place? It is not as if they need the supplementary income streams.

Nvidia, OpenAI and Anthropic all declined to comment, but it appears to be about brand promotion and reputation management.

Take US software firm Palantir Technologies, which has faced criticism due to it work for the military and police, both in the US and overseas. Since launching its own clothing range last year, Palantir now calls itself a "lifestyle brand".

Eliano Younes, Palantir's head of strategic engagement, says: "A lifestyle brand isn't defined by what you sell, it's defined by what you stand for and whether people want to affiliate with it. I believe that the store's success and the enthusiasm from our community proves this."

Younes adds that "investors, customers, employees, and everyday people" in more than 60 countries have bought Palantir's gear, which includes a cotton jacket.

Back at Nvidia, the popularity of its founder Huang may be driving the sale of its clothing. He has been known to attract crowds of adoring fans, competing for autographs or selfies with the 63-year-old who is known for his trademark leather jacket.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has described Huang as "Taylor Swift, but for tech".

Prof Gianpaolo Vignali of the Manchester Fashion Institute says: "People look at them [such big tech bosses] as role models. They want to aspire to them."

For Greg Epstein, author of the book Tech Agnostic, who describes the tech industry as a cult or new global religion, wearing tech merch is "a way of symbolising that you're one of the prophetic elite". This can particularly appeal to Silicon Valley insiders who are often "searching for a sense of identity, a sense of purpose, a sense of community".

Epstein, who is the humanist chaplain at both Harvard University and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, adds: "When tech bros put themselves on sweaters, it's more than just a cutesy phenomenon, it's an attempt to sell a cult whose goal is to radically alter the human condition."

Whether or not you choose to buy your next shirt or hat from a tech or defence firm, Vignali argues that all clothing choices are loaded with meaning. "The subtle colour of a tie or hair bobble… all of these are signals that allow the wearer to symbolically share their cultural and ideological positions," he says.

While tech and defence fashion seems to draw both ardent fans and fierce critics, not everyone takes it so seriously.

"It's a unique moment in our collective zeitgeist for sure," says Fratto, but she also thinks that Nvidia's decision to put Jensen Huang on the front of its official merch is also "kind of funny".

articles.title: OpenAI's Sam Altman says world 'right to be afraid' but 'should trust' AI firms
articles.text:
The boss of ChatGPT-maker OpenAI says people should have more faith in AI firms to keep the tech safe, amid rising public concerns about the risks.

"The world should trust that we are going to do the right thing because it's the right thing and we feel the magnitude of this," Sam Altman said on Tuesday during a conference in San Francisco.

He accepted people were justified in being concerned about AI, as the capability of the tools has progressed rapidly.

But critics say firms cannot be trusted to self-regulate, with left-wing Senator Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon, a former adviser of US President Donald Trump, among those calling for greater governance of AI.

Trump himself has criticised calls for more guardrails on the fast-moving technology, calling fears about AI's safety a "hoax".

He said the only "guardrails" needed for AI was a "strong and smart" president.

Altman's comments on Tuesday came during an appearance at an annual conference hosted by software firm Salesforce.

"It doesn't take as much imagination as it used to for [us] to imagine how this could go wrong," he said. "I think the world is right to be afraid of this."

But AI bosses themselves have also admitted it may be difficult to regulate a technology which is changing so quickly.

In an interview with Axios published on 3 September, external, Altman said he had expected Congress to create a "basic framework" for advanced AI after his 2023 testimony, but that has yet to happen.

He suggested lawmakers have struggled to keep pace with the technology and to regulate it without "slow[ing] down innovation".

New safety legislation on AI is unlikely to emerge from the US Congress anytime soon, despite the fact lawmakers returned from their summer break on Monday.

There is a lack of consensus within both US parties on how any regulation would happen - and the House is set to enter recess again at the end of the week ahead of the midterm elections in early November.

Altman's comments on Tuesday were the first time he had spoken publicly since a post went viral last week by a researcher who quit the AI firm Anthropic. The researcher claimed AI could "kill all humans" by the end of the decade if left unchecked.

A handful of other AI executives and experts responded by saying they agreed with the assessment, though they didn't explain how they came to their conclusions or how exactly AI could accomplish such a thing.

After Altman's comments, Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, external that every AI firm had the ability and the incentive "to take its own actions" towards safety.

"Any lab that doesn't focus on alignment will fall behind," the Meta chief executive wrote.

"Labs face significant liability if their models cause harm, so they have a strong incentive to prevent this as well."

Alignment is a field which aims to build human ethical ideas and principles into AI. In other words, it aims to keep it on track with what humans value.

Some political figures have pushed back against the view that AI firms should be able to self-regulate.

Bernie Sanders said decisions about AI had been left to "a handful of the richest people in the world", while former White House strategist Steve Bannon said the public could not trust tech oligarchs to regulate themselves.

Nvidia boss Jensen Huang said at the same conference on Tuesday that AI firms should decide if new versions of the technology should be released - and not be managed by outside forces.

"We don't need new laws or regulations," he said, adding there should not be a "false choice" between the speed of innovation and the safety of AI products.

Nvidia is the biggest company in the world by valuation, with its profits having boomed as a result of rampant demand for its hardware.

Huang also argued safety is an "engineering problem" and companies should "take a pause" if they lose confidence in a product.

The recent claims from inside the industry have intensified scrutiny of AI development, prompting Anthropic chief executive Dario Amodei to call for the pace of AI development to slow, external and urge governments to regulate the industry.

The post was applauded by Altman, Google's DeepMind co-founder Demis Hassabis and Elon Musk.

By Tuesday, however, more AI leaders were voicing support for self-regulation rather than government involvement.

Altman said AI companies were capable of regulating themselves.

"We will get it right," Altman said, adding that if firms could not keep "alignment and safety way ahead of capabilities" they would "slow down or stop".

But Yoshua Bengio, one of the pioneers of modern AI, posted on X, external "ambitious efforts outside the for-profit sector" were needed to "avert the worst risks from AI".

Leaders of OpenAI and Anthropic have said they have recently started working towards some sort of industry-wide agreement on safety.

Amodei, during a cameo at the conference on Tuesday, said Anthropic is now in "a dialogue with the rest of the industry" about committing to better safety standards and checks on AI tools and development.

He also said that one of the biggest surprises of the AI boom was not how the technology itself has advanced, but its broader impact.

"We didn't appreciate that it would lead to companies growing so fast, and how quickly they would become central to things," Amodei said.

OpenAI executive Chris Lehane said last week that the company was also working with other AI labs, external "to advance frontier AI standards, building a voluntary effort now, with or without government support." Those labs include Anthropic and Google Deepmind.

"With stakes this high, we cannot let the perfect become the enemy of the good," Lehane wrote.

articles.title: AI app ads promoting 'objectification of women' banned by watchdog
articles.text:
A series of social media adverts for AI apps have been banned by a UK watchdog for promoting "the creation of sexually explicit content and objectification of women".

The Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) said five ads uploaded to Meta platforms for AI companion and video generating apps had objectified and sexualised women, including through harmful gender stereotypes.

One of the ads used sexualised images of a girl under 18 to promote an AI companion app - while others invited users to upload images of their "crush" and turn images into "sizzling" videos.

Meta had already removed the offending ads. But Nicky Baker of the ASA said such content had the potential "to cause real-world harm".

"We take a firm line on ads that are likely to cause serious or widespread offence and these ads are a clear example of why that matters," she said.

"Encouraging and condoning the objectification of women and the creation of explicit content from people's images has the potential to cause real-world harm."

The ASA also said many of the ads it banned had promoted the creation of sexually explicit content using real women's images without their consent.

It comes only months after the UK outlawed apps to create non-consensual deepfake nude imagery - sparked by outrage over X's chatbot Grok complying with requests to nudify images of women on the platform.

The ASA said the law had changed during its investigations and that ads identified in future would be considered in light of both the law and its own rules.

Where ads are identified as illegal, it said it may notify platforms and law enforcement.

The ads were identified by the regulator using its AI-powered "Active Ad Monitoring System", which proactively searches for ads which might violate UK rules.

It said the five ads it were banned had depicted women irresponsibly, and were likely to cause serious or widespread offence.

One ad for an AI companion generator, developed by Animcha Ltd, was also found to have portrayed someone under 18 in a sexual way, the ASA said.

It presented the synthetic female character as someone users could "customise" and instruct, combining sexualised imagery with childlike clothing and objects.

Two ads for an AI portrait generation tool called Nexaipic encouraged users to "upload your crush and let AI create what you imagine" with sexually explicit videos.

An ad for an AI image-to-video generation app, identified only as KH31 DD22, depicted a clothed woman being transformed into a video in which she was topless.

The watchdog said this suggested the app could be used to create content that exposed women's bodies.

Further adverts for image generation tool Rusto AI, which encouraged users to create sexualised videos from photographs, were found to have condoned the digital manipulation of women's images to create sexually explicit content.

And an ad for an AI image-to-video generation app PictoPop used sexualised imagery to demonstrate the tool, including by portraying the woman in a submissive position.

The ASA said none of the apps' creators responded to its enquiries.

articles.title: Pubs in England and Wales to allow digital ID apps to prove age
articles.text:
Alcohol buyers will be able to use a digital ID app on their phones to prove their age under new rules introduced on Tuesday.

Pubs and shops in England and Wales can use the tech in addition to current physical forms of ID - with the government saying a digital option will make age-checks quicker and more secure for customers and staff.

Customers will be able to choose ID apps from a range of suppliers such as the Post Office, Yoti or Luciditi, provided they are on a government-approved list.

The change means businesses will no longer be required to let people use physical ID, but the government contends most establishments would.

The plan will be technology-agnostic, meaning that the government is not setting out in detail how each app must work.

It argues that under the voluntary digital ID scheme, drinkers would share fewer personal details with a venue or shop - such as tapping their phone on a reader or displaying a scannable QR code rather than handing over an official document.

The apps will also need to guard against customers borrowing devices from older friends and relatives, and ensure the ID app belongs to the person using it.

Yoti's digital ID app, for example, will only let a user log in if a scan of their face matches that of the person who signed up for the app.

The app then generates a QR code that can be scanned by a business with a free checker app, which tells them the person's age.

This is time-limited to make duping or sharing the QR code more difficult.

Digital government minister Stephanie Peacock said having the option for digital ID would "mean you do not need to carry a physical ID, nor hand over sensitive personal information" meaning people could "feel safer on a night out'".

Allen Simpson, chief executive of trade body UKHospitality, said the new rules were a "positive step".

He added the industry would work with government to make sure the scheme's roll-out would not be "burdensome" for the hospitality sector.

This would include ensuring there were multiple options for suppliers and that it was cost-efficient, Simpson said.

articles.title: Lost Bowie tracks from 1960s released for first time
articles.text:
Ten years ago Alec Palao was casually flicking through a collection of old records when he noticed some faint pencil markings that were enough to draw a gasp. "Davie Jones," it read.

What he had found was musical gold: five unreleased songs by a young David Bowie, filed away under his birth name.

From Friday, those tracks, plus another five unreleased songs that came Palao's way after the initial discovery, will be available to buy and stream.

"They are probably the most visceral, raw you'll ever hear the man," said Palao, a music historian and archivist.

For the music industry, David Bowie is big business. He entered the mainstream with his 1969 single, Space Oddity, and went on to achieve 11 number one albums.

He died in 2016, but remains one of Britain's most recognisable cultural icons.

Six of the previously unreleased tracks from the new collection will be available on vinyl, tapping into Bowie's popularity in that format specifically. In 2022, Bowie was named the best-selling vinyl artist of the 21st century by Music Week, ahead of The Beatles.

"It's just a fascinating window into London in 1965 and its possibilities," said Palao.

In the early sixties, Bowie was a teenager, performing as Davie Jones at London clubs and dreaming of stardom. Many of the tracks he recorded in that period are either little known or lost to time.

But his first professional producer, Shel Talmy, had kept a recording from 1965 among his collection of material by other artists he had worked with: The Kinks; The Who; Manfred Mann; The Easybeats.

"I think it's wonderful that people can get to hear the early Davie Jones music," said Dana Gillespie, an early collaborator of Bowie's.

She met him after a performance at the Marquee Club in London when Bowie was 17.

"They're songs that don't really sound like David but it's him trying to find his voice. He was experimenting."

Gillespie became close friends with Bowie, eventually working with him on his "Ziggy Stardust" album. Talmy worked with both artists and Bowie's song "Andy Warhol", on his fourth studio album, was originally written for Gillespie.

"He was very driven," remembered Gillespie, who is still touring and making music at the age of 77.

"Some time in the sixties, he asked me to come and visit his parents. We were in his little house in Bromley, and when his parents left the room he turned to me and said: 'Whatever it takes, I want to get out of here.' And he did," she said.

It is a decade since Palao found the recordings. Since then, it has been a long process to bring them to market. The result is an album that he says is "absolutely pure rock 'n' roll".

"If you're looking for clues as to what he was to become, there's maybe less of that," said Palao, "but objectively speaking, I feel it's important stuff."

Gillespie is excited by one song in particular.

"There was a famous café called the Gioconda in Denmark Street where I often used to go with David," she said, recalling the centre of musical life in London in the 1960s.

"One day when I was sitting there, David rushed in and took me by the hand. He said: 'You have to hear this'.

"He ran with me around the corner and squeezed us into a small listening booth. I had one speaker and he had the other, and he played me 'I Pity The Fool'."

A remastered version of the song can be heard in the new album.

For music historians, fans of Bowie, and those who were there, the new album is another chance to reconnect with an enduring cultural icon.

"David always wanted to be a big star," said Gillespie. "I'm so happy that his early stuff hasn't been forgotten."

articles.title: Robert Kraft says Ed Sheeran asked him to donate $2m to aid after Macklemore backlash
articles.text:
Robert Kraft, the US stadium owner who had pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore removed as Ed Sheeran's opening act, says Sheeran asked him to match his own $2m (£1.5m) donation for "aid in the region".

It came after Macklemore said he would donate $1m (£750,000) to Palestinian organisations, challenging Kraft to match him.

Kraft, who owns the New England Patriots, wrote on Wednesday: "Earlier today, before Macklemore challenged me to match his donation, Ed called me and asked me to commit $2 million to match his donation to aid in the region to fight this humanitarian crisis.

"Ed now plans to reach out to other venue owners and our goal is to continue to work together to build bridges."

Are you an Ed Sheeran fan? Get in touch.

Kraft did not confirm whether he has agreed to make the $2m donation and where the funds would go, and this is the first time it has been suggested Sheeran had donated that sum.

The musician has not commented about any donation he is making or other philanthropic plans.

Kraft's comments came in his second statement this week on the controversy over Sheeran's US tour.

On Monday, he confirmed he had banned Macklemore from performing during the British singer's forthcoming shows at his Gillette Stadium near Boston.

Kraft, who is Jewish, accused the US rapper of hate speech during two previous support slots, where he called for "free Palestine" on stage and made other comments and showed images of Gaza.

Macklemore performed a song dedicated to pro-Palestinian protesters, and referred to "genocide" in Gaza, a description Israel rejects. The rapper also said criticism of Israel was not intended as criticism of "my Jewish brothers and sisters".

Macklemore was removed from the tour on Monday, sparking a backlash that included Sheeran's other support acts dropping out in protest.

Sheeran has said the decision to drop the rapper was made by his promoters, Messina Touring Group, not by him.

Messina Touring Group said Macklemore was dropped because some venues - such as Kraft's Gillette Stadium - would refuse to let the concerts take place if he performed, meaning the tour would have been cancelled if Macklemore remained on the bill.

Sheeran, who played at Kraft's wedding in 2022, has faced criticism from some for his apparent acceptance of the decision.

In his statement on Tuesday, the singer said he respects "Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes", and that while he doesn't use his own platform for politics, that "doesn't mean I don't care" or "support causes in my own, personal way".

The singer-songwriter also said he did not want to let down his fans or crew by cancelling the tour, which is set to resume in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, on Saturday.

Although some artists like Billy Bragg have called for Sheeran to scrap the tour, that would potentially leave the musician and his promoters liable for huge sums for costs including venue hire and ticket refunds.

Sheeran is able to perform solo, even if his set has to be reconfigured to compensate for the loss of Irish folk band Beoga, who previously accompanied him for several songs.

articles.title: Palace in war of words with Earl Spencer over book's claim on Charles and Diana
articles.text:
Buckingham Palace is in a war of words with Earl Spencer, brother of Diana, Princess of Wales, over a controversial memoir about her life and death.

King Charles III is accused of insensitively telling Earl Spencer, in the wake of Princess Diana's death in 1997, that "we'll forget her soon enough", according to excerpts in the Daily Mail.

But the Palace has pushed back unusually strongly, angered by the claims and attempting to cast doubt on them.

"While we do not comment on books as a matter of principle, His Majesty is mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways others do not recognise, even many years after such a loss," it said.

The language is reminiscent of Queen Elizabeth's unexpectedly firm response to claims of racism by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex in 2021, with the comment that "recollections may vary".

And the row threatens to overshadow a very crowded day for the royals - with the King, Prince William and Catherine attending events, and Prince Harry making his first big appearance since returning to the UK.

Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, to be published next week, seems set to reopen a very difficult time in the recent history of the Royal Family - written from the perspective of her own Spencer family.

The death of Princess Diana, a hugely popular figure, had created a volatile atmosphere, in which the royals were accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and had seemed out of touch with the public mood.

Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Princess Diana's sudden death. And this book will give an insider's view on those events.

In the published excerpt, Earl Spencer says the then-Prince of Wales subjected him to a "stream of anger" after he insisted Diana would not have wanted Princes William and Harry, then aged 15 and 12, to have to walk in her funeral procession.

Earl Spencer wrote in the book: "He [Charles] unleashed down the phone what I have always taken to be his pent-up contempt for Diana, and his horror that the world was so bowled over by her death. 'Rest assured,' he hissed, 'we'll forget her soon enough'."

It is a claim that is being rejected by the Palace, who see it as being entirely out of character for a man with a deeply compassionate nature, who at the time was dealing with his own grief and that of their two sons.

Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".

In 2017, he told the BBC he did not "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong" but. "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.

Earlier on Wednesday, it emerged that copies of Earl Spencer's unreleased book had been stolen from a lorry in the Netherlands.

Julian Payne, the monarch's former communications secretary, told the BBC that the King's apparent comments in the book were "just not language that I recognise".

He said the "highly unusual" statement from the Palace demonstrated the "strength of feeling that there must have been for them to feel that they needed to go out there and correct it".

The dispute comes when multiple royal events will be jostling for attention.

King Charles intervened in the debate about artificial intelligence on Thursday, calling on AI industry leaders to prevent it becoming a destructive force and warning of the potential "existential dangers" it could pose.

"Those who have created these technologies are now increasingly warning that AI risks developing darker capacities - perhaps even to take life," the King said as he hosted a gathering of leading AI firms at Dumfries House, in Ayrshire.

"In this regard, if I may say so, there seems urgency in adequately considering the existential dangers of such technologies falling into the wrong hands, and being used in potentially catastrophic ways."

articles.title: Eurovision: Ireland boycotts contest for second year in a row
articles.text:
Irish broadcaster RTÉ will not broadcast or participate in the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest.

It is the second year in a row that the broadcaster has not participated in the competition.

In 2026, RTÉ withdrew from the 2026 contest in Vienna, after the European Broadcasting Union confirmed that Israeli public broadcaster KAN would be allowed to take part.

In a statement they said: "RTÉ feels that Ireland's participation cannot be justified given the appalling and ongoing loss of lives in Gaza and the humanitarian crisis there which continues to put the lives of so many civilians at risk."

Last year Ireland, Spain, the Netherlands and Slovenia boycotted the Eurovision Song Contest, after it was decided Israel could compete.

RTÉ added that they also remain "deeply concerned by the continued denial of independent access to international journalists to the territory".

Ireland has won the competition seven times between 1970 and 1996, a joint record holder alongside Sweden.

articles.title: GTA 6 album: Soundtrack reveal revives digital release debate
articles.text:
The reveal of a Grand Theft Auto 6 soundtrack album has reignited a debate over the decision not to release the game on disc.

Developer Rockstar Games announced a 34-track compilation, set to release on CD and vinyl on the same day as the highly anticipated video game.

The company says it will include original music from a "genre-defying roster of the most exciting artists in the world" including rapper Travis Scott, country singer Morgan Wallen and UK singer PinkPantheress.

But some fans have pointed out the "irony" of putting out a physical edition of the album following its controversial decision for a digital-only release of the game.

The first six tracks, published at the time of the announcement, also include rapper Yung Lean, British DJ Fred Again and Rolling Stone Keith Richards.

GTA games feature multiple radio stations, usually themed around a particular musical genre, which players can switch between while driving.

In the past the game's soundtracks have largely been made up of licensed music from established artists, although original songs have also featured.

Rockstar has said the upcoming game will feature a "dynamic score" and "evolution of in-game radio".

Being included in a Grand Theft Auto game can bring a new generation of fans to an artist's music.

Spotify streams of Tom Petty's Love is a Long Road, the track used in GTA 6's first trailer, increased by 36,979% after the clip was published.

Hot Together, by the Pointer Sisters, also saw a huge jump when it soundtracked the game's second trailer.

And a collection of tracks used in the recent Extended Look attracted new listeners in the week after it premiered on Netflix.

According to music and gaming publication MusicEXP, external, pop duo Captain & Tennille's 1980 track But I Think It's a Dream saw the biggest spike, jumping from 70 Spotify streams in one week to 80,744.

Cliff Richard's Devil Woman was streamed more than one million times, while Prefab Sprout's Cars and Girls jumped from 49K to 187K additional weekly streams.

It also noted increases in activity on music detection app Shazam around tracks featured in the 26-minute broadcast.

Some artists have refused to let Rockstar use their music in GTA games.

Martyn Ware, from synth pop band Heaven 17, called the developer out on social media, accusing them of offering a "pitiful" deal to use 1983 hit Temptation.

articles.title: Ed Sheeran's persona as music's Mr Nice Guy worsened the biggest crisis of his career
articles.text:
Singer Ed Sheeran is facing the biggest controversy of his career after a storm over a decision to drop support act Macklemore from his US stadium tour following the rapper's on-stage pro-Palestinian comments.

Sheeran is one of the most successful songwriters of all time. He has sold more than 120 million records and spent more than 1,000 weeks on the US album charts.

Part of his appeal - apart from those insidiously catchy songs - is his everyman persona. He looks and dresses like a fan on the train home from Glastonbury, rather than one of the festival's headliners.

He has carefully cultivated a non-threatening, everyone welcome public image. In 2014, he donated his entire wardrobe to charity shops. The same year, he adopted a one-month-old kitten, saving it from euthanasia, and named it Graham. Today, he runs a charity providing music lessons to under-18s in his home county of Suffolk.

He tries to stay out of politics - usually only getting involved to campaign for issues like copyright protection and ticket touting, or to raise concerns over the impact of Brexit on touring musicians.

But like most artists, he leans left. In 2017, he said he supported then-Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, despite not endorsing him at the stump.

"People thought that, because I didn't put myself behind him, I wasn't a Corbyn supporter," Sheeran told the Sunday Times. "If you knew me as a person, and listened to my music, you would be able to make a pretty educated guess that he would be the kind of person I really dig."

When it comes to non-musical issues, Sheeran prefers to remain circumspect. His reasoning, he says, is that music should unite. He views his concerts as a "place of safety and sanctuary" built on shared humanity.

This week, that argument has come crumbling down - creating a crisis for his reputation and career.

By now, you probably know the story. Macklemore was picked as opening act on Sheeran's US tour, and on the first night made a speech saying "Free Palestine" and showing images of the destruction in Gaza.

The following night, he referred to the death toll as a genocide, a claim that Israel rejects.

He faced condemnation, with the organisation StopAntisemitism accusing Macklemore of "ambushing" the audience. Stadium owners, apparently led by the billionaire owner of the New England Patriots, Robert Kraft, put pressure on Sheeran and his promoters to drop him from the tour.

After a week of backroom discussions, they got their way.

On Tuesday, Sheeran issued a statement saying the decision was made by the promoters, not by him.

He said he had tried to build bridges between the parties, to no avail. And he said he was "not complicit", arguing that his decision to remain out of the Middle East debate in public wasn't proof he "didn't care".

"I am appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestine," he wrote. "The suffering and pain caused on both sides is a human tragedy. There are too many wars across the world causing immeasurable pain, none of which should be tolerated."

He continued: "There is a reason I do not use my professional platform for politics - my audience includes young people, often children, of all backgrounds."

The statement landed with a thud.

If Sheeran is so concerned about children, critics said, how come he hasn't mentioned the thousands of children killed in Gaza?

Others pointed out that his abstention from politics was not absolute. He wore a "justice for Grenfell" T-shirt at Wembley Stadium in 2018 after the Grenfell Tower fire, played the Concert For Ukraine in 2022, and recorded a protest song about the Ukraine war with U2 earlier this year.

Questions were also raised about his relationship with Kraft. Sheeran sang at the businessman's wedding in 2022, and in a subsequent interview called him "super sweet".

Music journalist Jeffrey Ingold said Sheeran's apparent acceptance of the decision to drop Macklemore seemed like "cowardice".

"He is one of the biggest musicians in the world," Ingold told BBC Radio 5 Live. "He has power and he has leverage. And he has essentially washed his hands and said, this is not my responsibility.

"He had options, right? He could have said to the promoters and the owners of the venues, including Robert Kraft, 'You know what, we're not going to do the shows there. If you're not going to let us all perform, we're not going to do it'. He could have found alternate venues."

Hours after Sheeran's statement landed, his tour went into crisis. All three support acts for the remaining shows - Finneas, Aaron Rowe and Lukas Graham - pulled out, voicing support for Macklemore. Beoga - who back Sheeran to play songs like Galway Girl and Nancy Mulligan - also quit.

Many of them said Macklemore's axing, at the hands of a group of billionaire venue owners, represented a chilling effect on free speech.

Others from music and beyond have spoken out. Pop star Pink, who is Jewish, reposted an anti-Macklemore meme and then her own message, explaining why she was critical of the rapper's comments.

Suddenly, against his will, Sheeran has become the centre of a political storm over one of the world's most divisive issues.

Could Sheeran have handled it better when the controversy blew up? Absolutely.

In his statement, he said he wanted to continue the tour, to avoid letting down fans and the crew who rely on his concerts to make a living.

If he had threatened to pull the plug on the shows, he could have framed it as a protest for free speech - although that would still inevitably have been interpreted as an endorsement of Macklemore's statements.

So, Sheeran stumbled into a Catch 22 situation. He was damned either way.

His nice guy image has taken a huge dent, and the "not my responsibility" tone of his statement certainly didn't help.

Ingold says: "I think it will change the way people look at him and see him from this point forward.

"He has said he's not complicit, but he actually is incredibly complicit in what's happening [on this tour]."

Jem Aswad, executive music editor of Variety, says the episode shows "you can't be neutral on this issue" - but points out that most people don't go to Sheeran's concerts to be reminded of issues like Gaza, "they go there to stop thinking about it and be entertained".

Aswad doubts that this controversy will cause his career major damage, saying he doesn't think most of the criticism "is necessarily coming from Ed Sheeran's fans".

"It's coming from people who object to the way that he's behaved in this [situation], and I'm not sure a lot of those people are really Ed Sheeran's fans."

We'll find out when Sheeran plays his next show in Philadelphia on Saturday. A vocal contingent might make their thoughts known, but many will just be turning up to enjoy the music.

The loss of his backing band isn't the disaster it may seem, either.

On previous tours, Sheeran has been the only artist on stage - accompanying himself on a loop pedal instead of relying on other musicians.

But once this run of concerts ends in Mexico this December, his next steps will have to be carefully planned.

Perhaps, in an age of febrile discontent, staying above the fray is simply impossible.

articles.title: Hertfordshire boy, 13, is new voice of Thomas the Tank Engine
articles.text:
A 13-year-old schoolboy has made his voice-acting debut as Thomas the Tank Engine in a new animated series.

Harry Sparkes, from Harpenden, Hertfordshire, stars in Thomas & Friends: Railway Stories alongside Crazy Rich Asians actor Henry Golding, who narrates the series in a role made famous by Sir Ringo Starr.

For nine months, Sparkes kept his weekly recording sessions secret from his classmates by telling them he was attending physiotherapy for a foot injury.

"It feels amazing, because I played and watched Thomas as a kid, and now I get to be Thomas. It just feels insane," he said.

Sparkes added that he thought his friends would be shocked to find out he was voicing the character.

He said he was excited he got "to be part of something which kids from the next generation will get to grow up to watch".

Franchise owners Mattel teased the new series will "introduce fans to a refreshed world of Sodor, while still celebrating the iconic railway action we have all known and loved since its debut as a classic book in 1945".

articles.title: Bonnie Greer: British-American author and critic dies aged 77
articles.text:
British-American author and cultural commentator Bonnie Greer has died at the age of 77 after a brief illness, her husband has said.

In a statement delivered with "profound sadness", Greer's widower David Hutchins noted how the acclaimed playwright and critic had made "an enduring contribution to British cultural and public life" with her "intelligence, courage and distinctive voice".

He added: "To me, she was my partner, confidante and inspiration, and I feel profoundly privileged to have shared my life with her."

Hutchins continued: "Those closest to Bonnie will remember her warmth, humour, generosity and extraordinary ability to bring people together."

BBC presenter Clive Myrie led the tributes from elsewhere, posting on X: "This is such a shock. She was a friend and mentor and I will miss her with all my heart."

Former deputy prime minister David Lammy called Greer "a powerful wordsmith and artist, she was eloquent and exacting".

He added that she was "a true life force" and he would "never forget her quiet fearlessness taking on Nick Griffin" during an appearance with the then-British National Party (BNP) leader on the BBC's Question Time in 2009.

Lammy added: "I will miss her mentorship, and her friendship."

London Mayor Sadiq Khan said Greer's voice brought "courage, humour and humanity to Britain's cultural conversation".

He said: "She inspired and opened doors for so many others. And she was great fun too - I will miss her friendship enormously."

Born in Chicago in 1948, Greer wrote plays from a young age and went on to study theatre in her home city and before attending the Actors Studio in New York with director Elia Kazan.

Greer moved to the UK in 1986 and became a familiar face on UK TV, appearing as a frequent panellist on programmes like Question Time and Newsnight Review, debating the topics of the day.

She penned award-winning works like Munda Negra, which won her the Verity Bargate Award for best play, and novels such as Hanging by Her Teeth (1994) and Entropy (2009).

Once named by the Observer, external as one of the country's leading public intellectuals, Greer's work - across a range of disciplines and platforms - often tackled issues around culture, race and public institutions.

Speaking to the Guardian, external in 2016 in the aftermath of the Black Lives Matter movement, Greer said: "When I wake up in the morning, I'm just myself. It's only when I leave the door that I become a black woman to the world."

She added: "I tell black women all the time, 'Don't apologise for yourself and keep your hair nappy. Make sure you are heard'."

Greer served on the boards of cultural institutions including the British Museum, Royal Opera House and London Film School, and was chancellor of London's Kingston University.

Her other published works include a memoir titled A Parallel Life and a biography of US poet and playwright Langston Hughes.

Also in 2009, her part-memoir, part-music-history book, Obama Music, was published.

Greer was made an OBE in 2010 for services to the arts.

In 2022, she was appointed as a fellow of the Royal Society of Literature.

Broadcaster and author John Simpson added to the tributes on Wednesday, posting: "So sad to hear of the death of the writer and critic Bonnie Greer.

"She was a good friend, and gave me strong support at a time I needed it. Fiercely intelligent, but always avoided personal attacks. A huge loss."

Fellow journalist and broadcaster Sangita Myska, who interviewed Greer several times, recalled her as having been a "smart, sassy, firebrand who will be missed from our public discourse".

articles.title: Ex-BBC presenter John Humphrys questions role of Royal Family in new documentary
articles.text:
Veteran broadcaster John Humphrys has said the people of the United Kingdom should "be able to choose our leaders" as he releases a documentary exploring the role of the Royal Family.

Humphrys, who for decades was one of the most prominent faces on the BBC, is presenting a new Channel 4 documentary called The Royals: Time to Go?

Speaking to BBC Radio Wales Breakfast, the Cardiff-born presenter said he "admires" King Charles III in many ways, but said it was a "matter of choice".

Buckingham Palace has been approached for comment.

In the documentary, Humphrys speaks to both critics and supporters of the monarchy, and makes the case for electing a president as the head of state.

He recalled seeing the late Queen Elizabeth II visiting Cardiff when he was growing up, watching her being driven down Newport Road.

"My father didn't attend and said he would never bend the knee to anyone. I guess that rubbed off on me," he said.

Humphrys asked why it was seen as such a taboo to call for an alternative to the Royal Family, saying that "we can because it's a democracy".

"I know the monarch is not a political leader, but he is our leader, and we need to bow our knee to him.

"That's what I object to. Shouldn't we get a choice?"

He met the Queen throughout his career, including at Buckingham Palace where he said he spoke to her "and the corgis of course".

Humphrys, who presented the Nine O'Clock News, the Today programme and Mastermind throughout a decades-long career with the corporation, said he took the opportunity to ask her for an interview.

"When I'd finished, she looked up at me and said just one word 'no' and I thought I could build on that," he said.

articles.title: Olu Jacobs: Legendary Nollywood actor dies in Nigeria aged 84
articles.text:
Olu Jacobs, one of Nigeria's best known actors, whose career spanned several decades across theatre, television and film, has died at the age of 84.

His wife, veteran actress Joke Silva, announced his death and asked for privacy while the family mourns.

Silva announced his passing in a statement describing the celebrated actor as "The Lion of Lufodo" and saying his life was "well lived and fought".

Some of his notable films include My Kingdom, Covert Operation and One Fine Day.

He was regarded as one of the father figures of Nollywood, as Nigeria's film industry in known, commanding widespread respect and admiration across the country.

"We call on all bloggers and social media influencers to respect our family's privacy at this time," Silva said in a statement.

Born on 11 July 1942, Jacobs was trained at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London before embarking on a career that included appearances in British television productions and international films.

He became one of the defining figures of Nigeria's film industry, appearing in numerous Nigerian productions and earning recognition for his commanding screen presence and versatility.

His career spanned more than five decades, during which he received several major honours, including the African Movie Academy Award for Best Actor in a Leading Role and lifetime achievement honours.

In 2011, Jacobs was conferred with the national honour of Member of the Order of the Federal Republic (MFR) in recognition of his contribution to the Nigerian film industry.

Jacobs and Silva jointly established the Lufodo Group and Lufodo Academy of Performing Arts, contributing not only to film and television but also to developing and training performing artists in Nigeria.

In recent years, Jacobs had largely stayed away from the public spotlight due to ill-health.

In 2021, Silva disclosed that he had been diagnosed with Dementia with Lewy bodies.

"It's a degenerative disease that affects the brain and it's almost like a Parkinson-type of disease - it affects the brain and affects the person," she said in an interview with Nigerian broadcaster Chude Jideonwo.

On several occasions, there were rumours that Jacobs had died, but his family would promptly debunk them, the latest being in June 2024 when his eldest son, Soji, went on TV to say his father was still alive.

articles.title: Beck: ‘What does a devil’s haircut look like? Anything with a lot of architecture and wild flights of fancy’
articles.text:
You’ve been performing since the late 80s. What keeps you going? AmongstTheWaves

It’s a good question. I don’t really know any other life. I’ve spent a lot of my time trying to create a body of work, and out of that, maybe there’s a few songs at the end that are not bad. So I just keep going down into the mine, trying to come back with a couple of things worth keeping. It’s a lot of digging. If I had to stop and get a job painting houses or something, I would still make songs just for myself, because that’s how it started.

You tend to alternate between styles from album to album. What do you feel is closer to your intrinsic self, funky Beck or lonesome Beck? Mazzini

Probably lonesome. But the other side of things gets me out of my shell, stops me from being a little too ponderous, which I’m apt to do. The other side of what I do – Loser or Odelay – was more of a fluke. At the time that was what people liked. Now it’s kind of reversed – they prefer the more introspective, quiet songs, and stuff that’s a little more genreless. I don’t have any songs that they play at weddings, like Uptown Funk. I remember telling Mark Ronson, “Hey, you made a wedding song.” He was like, “Yeah, finally.” That’s a very elite category of song.

Your interview with Thurston Moore on MTV in 1994 is one of the most gloriously ramshackle interviews ever. Were you both doing a bit? LoftyDog

We filmed a bunch of things they wouldn’t air because they thought they would get in trouble or get sued by people. I’d brought an old-fashioned telephone and at one point we pulled out some baseball bats and destroyed the phone. I don’t remember what the bit was – who was calling us? Whatever it was, we decided to smash the phone in reaction to a call. We were kind of doing performance art. I met a lot of resistance and ridicule for being like that on my first album. I would do interviews and say wild things because so much of it was boring, just rote questions – and I thought if my friends are reading this, they’d be bored to death.

A lot of the things on TV were just going through the motions. As a kid, every once in a while I’d see something that jarred me. Like, wow, there was a glitch in the system and something real broke through. Something genuine that reminded us that this is all a construct, this smooth oiled machine that provides content for us. It was a very youthfully exuberant attempt to try to disrupt everything that was very pre-programmed and uninteresting. Thurston and I both came from underground art backgrounds, so it was preposterous to be allowed on mainstream TV. We were like, let’s seize the moment and do something.

Given how productive you were right from the start of your career, how did you feel about being tagged with the “slacker rock” label? SalfordianBlue

I thought it was a reductive term. There was this influx of all this underground music that had been bubbling through the 80s and early 90s, and it all hit the mainstream at once. One day it was Vanilla Ice and hair metal and Whitney Houston, and then the next day it was Nirvana and all the stuff that you would see at your local dive bar. The 80s had been very curated and airbrushed and brightly coloured – I remember the first time I went to a record label, they told me I looked messy and rough, and it would never work. Whoever that was missed the point. We were reacting to how cleaned up everything was, and going back to something a little more raw and real.

To many, Loser felt like a classic one-hit wonder. Did you always have faith that you’d have a long career in music? StayPositive

I never had any expectations. I think the thing that supersedes everything is whether you are writing good songs. The people I came up with who wrote good songs – they’re the ones that are still around and playing arenas and stadiums. And it was tricky when I was coming up, writing a catchy song was frowned upon. If you had anything that was too poppy or catchy, you were selling out, it wasn’t real art. What’s funny is the catchiest, poppiest songs from that time are the ones that everybody loves now.

What would a devil’s haircut look like, and have you ever seen someone sporting one? StayPositive

It’d probably have a little bit of a rockabilly edge. Somebody showed me a video once of these proto-punk type people in Australia called sharpies, and they had a bizarre version of a mullet. It was really short bangs and kind of draped in the back. Something like that, maybe. I have a book of hairstyle photos that they would use in 80s hair salons – there are a lot of devil’s haircuts. I think any haircut that has a lot of architecture to it, with wild flights of fancy.

In their 1998 hit You Get What You Give the New Radicals threatened to kick the asses of Hanson, Courtney Love, Marilyn Manson – and Beck. Did they ever catch up with you? Dave_Rowlinson

I ran into [New Radicals songwriter Gregg Alexander] in an Erewhon [health food supermarket] at the time, and he said: “I’m a big fan. We should write together.” And I just looked at him like, “What do you …? What’s happening here?” I thought the song was a little corny at the time, but it’s probably a classic now. It’s pretty catchy. I think the chords, to me, were a little too fancy for the aesthetic of the time.

Are you still in touch with [producer duo] the Dust Brothers? You’re one of the last artists who worked with them, on Gueroin 2005, before they vanished into thin air. I genuinely wonder what happened to them! Coopertapes

I did actually see them about a year ago. I see them from time to time. We have unfinished records that were never put out, so who knows? Maybe there’ll be something down the road. I’ve never asked, but I’m guessing they don’t really need to work in music, they’re doing other things. They worked with Hanson right after Odelay – people thought we were related [Beck’s surname is Hansen]. I remember they were working on that, the Rolling Stones and the Fight Club soundtrack. So that’s why my next two albums were not fully produced by the Dust Brothers, after the success of Odelay they became too busy.

Looking to the future, do you see yourself sharing the stage with a chain-smoking alcoholic robot? AKA how did you come to be a guest star on Futurama? vammyp

They wrote a script and sent it to me, and I said no. Through that whole era, I said no to pretty much everything. I was asked to do the theme for Austin Powers 2 and 3, and Shrek, and I was even saying no to, like, Amores Perros and Y Tu Mamá También and Run Lola Run, all these classic movies. They wanted me to act in High Fidelity and Ghost World, and I just decided that I didn’t want to “go Hollywood”.

They sent me this cartoon and I thought, well, if I did something like this it would be The Simpsons – a lot of people have done that, Sonic Youth have done that. The script was sitting on the tour bus, and my band got a hold of it on a long drive and said, “What is this?” And I said, “Oh, it’s this show, Futurama. I’ve never heard of it, but they want me to do this ridiculous thing.” And they said, “You have to do it!” They all ganged up on me so I did it.

Beercan is my go-to “shake your ass” number. What is yours? TeeDubyaBee

I would say anything from the early 80s funk era. Anything Sly Stone, James Brown – and early 80s Prince era, Talking Heads. Classics.

Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind is one of my favourite films, and your recording of Everybody’s Got to Learn Sometime is a sublime part of it. How did you get involved with the film, and why that song in particular? Cybillservice

I did a music video with Michel Gondry, the director, and we became pals. I was having dinner over at his house one night, and he described this convoluted plot that I couldn’t quite follow. I said, “I don’t totally understand what this is, but when you make it, I want to see it.” Three or four years later, he called me up and said, “I made the movie.” My buddy Jon Brion was doing the score. It’s one of the only things, again, that I said yes to. But it was because it was a personal relationship. It’s become one of my songs that people love the most. I had just done Sea Change, which I think is one of the reasons they called me. That album had met so much shock from my fans that I swore to never make a record like that again. And now it’s beloved. It’s probably the main thing that people care about. I don’t think anybody’s mentioned Odelay to me in years, it’s all Sea Change and Midnite Vultures.

articles.title: ‘I thank God for killing me and bringing me back’: Nicolas Winding Refn on the heart surgery that inspired his new sci-fi horror
articles.text:
Nicolas Winding Refn has his phone out, showing me one of the goriest scenes he’s ever been involved in. Given that the Danish director’s movies have involved hands getting sliced off, eyeballs being gouged out and a son reaching deep inside his mother’s womb, that’s certainly saying something. In this video, the camera is fixed upon a beating heart when suddenly – slash! – it gets sliced open with a knife. We travel into the open chamber, as needles arrive to pierce through the muscle. Unsettling and compelling, could this be a future Palme d’Or winner?

Unlikely. You see, Refn isn’t the director of this footage; he’s actually the guy lying conked out in the operating room while a surgeon attends to him. Requesting that someone films your own heart surgery is a very Nicolas Winding Refn thing to do. “At first they said no,” says the film-maker known for Drive, Bronson and The Neon Demon. “But then they said, ‘As it’s you, we’ll record it.’”

Sitting in a swanky London hotel bar, drinking espressos and wearing a smart blue polo shirt under a skinny suit, Refn is here to talk about his latest movie, Her Private Hell, a ludicrously camp dream-collage of sci-fi, horror, spoof and revenge set in neon-lit Tokyo. But for the first 40 minutes of our chat, he recounts – with precious little interruption from me – the story of the 2023 operation that saved his life. Without it, he says, Her Private Hell would never have been made – not so much on health grounds, but because, before he was given this second chance at life, he had lost the passion for making movies.

“When you’re young, your creative flame is bright red,” he says. “But my own flame had vanished, like tears in the rain. I had fallen into a form of abyss. I was 50 years old and had no idea what to do with my remaining years.”

The story begins in summer 2023, when Refn was working on a Prada campaign in Italy. He was feeling increasingly tired, and his daughter mentioned how pale he appeared, but he put it down to overwork. It was only after he returned to his home in Copenhagen that a doctor examined him and discovered that a valve in his heart was broken, and filling his lungs with blood. “I was essentially dying,” says Refn. They told him to come back in two weeks for open heart surgery, and gave him a choice of replacement valve: metal or pig.

Her Private Hell stars Sophie Thatcher as Elle, an actor hoping to rebuild her relationship with her film mogul father by making her own Barberella-style sci-fi film: throughout the movie, you’re never quite sure if what you’re watching is the actual plot, or scenes from the fictional movie, or one of the characters’ fever dreams. That’s pretty much how I feel listening to Refn’s tale of heart surgery, which he has transformed into some kind of epic cinematic quest.

He mentions the quality of the light, the long silences (both features of his movies), and describes himself pleading to a higher power like George Bailey in It’s A Wonderful Life (his favourite film of all time): “Like, please God, just give me five more minutes, man!”

Refn was told to write a will and says he “made peace” with his wife: “I said, it’s been 30 years, we had a good run at it, but like tears in the rain, everything has an end.” (He really does love that Blade Runner quote.) He says he went through all the typical emotions: fear, anger, sadness, desperation. Not that anyone would have known.

“I didn’t make a fuss about it,” he says, “because I’m like a superhero.”

The lowest point came when he met a man who was fresh from similar open heart surgery. “He looked like he’d been in a boxing match with Mike Tyson,” says the director, who wasn’t keen on ageing a decade overnight.

But just as all heroes suffer setbacks, they eventually rise to conquer them. Just before the operation, Refn received a phone call from his surgeon that would change everything. “He was the Tom Cruise of surgeons,” says Refn, somewhat lustily. “He rode a motorbike, he had rings, he was very sexy. All the nurses said, ‘Oh my God, you’re getting him. You’re so lucky!’”

Sexy Tom Cruise told Refn that he could fix him in a way no other doctor in Copenhagen could – through telescopic surgery, which meant not needing to open up his ribcage. Refn believes it was divine intervention. “I think God was trying to tell me something. He’s saying, ‘You’re not ready to go yet, kid. But you’re going to go through a challenging process to reignite whatever that is inside of you.’”

By the time his operation came around, Refn says he was already a different person: “I was a champ, a winner. The nurses prepare you for how your life will probably change afterwards. But I remember telling them that, actually, this was the best thing ever in my life. And that they were not to worry because my sex drive was going to be times a thousand when I was back.” Er, was that an issue before? He pauses and smiles. “No. It actually ended the conversation. But it was a way to show how [the operation] was about rebirth, regeneration.”

When Refn was washed and shaved for the operation, he saw it in quasi-religious terms: he was rinsing his past away. In the eerily empty hospital, he remembers feeling full of cinematic emotion when someone from LA, who had no idea what Refn was going through, called to ask “a random question”. They ruined a key scene in your movie! “Yeah, it was kind of like somebody getting up to buy more popcorn in the final farewell scene,” he says.

Refn may have avoided fighting Tyson but his operation was no walk in the park: he remembers “incredible physical pain”, and it took three months to rebuild himself. He says he was like an infant, learning to do things for the first time again. But when it came to film-making, that proved to be an advantage.

In Her Private Hell – which is chiefly about the protective relationship between father and daughter – we meet Private K, played by Charles Melton, an American GI in postwar Japan searching for his lost daughter. Private K believes she was taken by a mythical figure known as the Leatherman, who is said to roam Tokyo ripping open girls’ chests with his diamond-studded gloved hands (no prizes for guessing what inspired that particular method of execution).

The character of Private K came from Refn realising that, while his eldest daughter, Lola, had recently left home, his youngest, Lizzielou, was only 12 and still needed him around. “Private K’s story was a cinematic narrative I could cling on to, my fantasy version of what happened to me.”

Refn’s films often contain echoes from his previous movies, and Her Private Hell is no different, in particular sharing a line from Only God Forgives, in which a father is told: “You should have protected her.” This clearly taps into a fear of Refn’s: that he won’t be able to. “I call it ‘dadsploitation’,” he says, with a hint of a smile. “It’s a form of fetish that appeals to men, that you are basically allowed to indulge in extreme biblical violence to protect innocence, especially when it comes to your daughter. Every father’s worst nightmare is something happening to their daughter of a sexual nature, and it gives a kind of permission: it gives me the authority to tear you to pieces in a biblical way, and I will enjoy every minute of it. Lots of films do it.”

I did wonder if this message taps into current rightwing tropes: from Trump’s fetishisation of muscle-bound “real men” to the anti-immigrant activists who claim they want to “save our girls”. But Refn says he’s not a politician selling a message. “All I know is that all humans want a hero. And I believe that for fathers, whether you’re left or right, we all have the same primal instinct inside us.”

He doesn’t seem like a macho guy, though. “I’m a very unmacho guy,” he says. “I love femininity. I love flamboyance. I love camp. I love colour. Her Private Hell is my version of playing with dolls. Everyone’s dressed up in uniforms, I get to move these girls around in fabulous clothes, and I get to take Charles Melton’s shirt off and show his ripped body like an action figure.”

It’s certainly outrageously camp at times. Elle’s movie mogul father is a ridiculous figure named Johnny Thunders (yes, he’s a Heartbreakers fan) who wears leather trousers and lights matches on his neck stubble. Throughout the film we hear leather garments stretch and bodily joints crack. “I love fetish,” says Refn. “Those sounds are incredibly erotic.”

Back in the 90s, when Refn was an enfant terrible making the gritty Danish drug drama Pusher, he considered himself “a Sex Pistol of cinema, there to fight for teenagers against the system, making things that would piss off their parents. But you grow out of that because everyone my age starts doing their gardening.” He smiles, then adds. “Except me, because I don’t garden.”

Now, he says, the “system” has been replaced with new enemies: social media, AI, tech overlords. Her Private Hell, Refn says with confidence, is “a movie that AI could never do. It’s the enemy of the algorithm. Because it’s not one movie, it’s five movies in one.”

“Most entertainment today is like this,” he adds, holding a white napkin up to his face. “A white sheet with codes on it. You don’t even need to pay attention, you can do a lot of other things at the same time. I don’t think that’s particularly healthy for the mind or the soul.”

His films, he says, are more like fairytales: simplistic enough to read to a child, yet bottomless in interpretation. “That’s why people still examine Hans Christian Andersen. But we’ve forgotten this because our entertainment is based on just giving and receiving information.”

Not everyone agrees with his assessment: reviews for Her Private Hell have been wildly mixed. In fact, it’s hard to think of a film-maker who splits opinion so consistently. Depending on who you listen to, Refn movies are either gorgeously shot, hypnotic meditations on the human psyche, or tedious borefests full of style and zero substance.

Refn claims not to care. In fact, he says he would hate it if everyone loved his movies. “It would be devastating. I would be very depressed,” he says. “If we like something and we all agree on it in this room, it’s as if we don’t like it. But if one likes it and one doesn’t and we end up arguing about it, that’s passion. That means that we have been penetrated.”

He points to Raging Bull: “Commercially bad. Very divisive at the time. Now you would say, ‘How can you make anything better?’ Opinions disappear, like tears in the rain, but passion will still exist.”

He sighs, reflecting on the reaction to his film’s Cannes premiere. “A lot of people had a meltdown again. It’s like, here we go again, ‘There’s no storyline!’ And I’m like, ‘You’re so wrong! There’s so much going on, you’re just looking in the wrong places.’”

The kids are far smarter than critics, he says. “They feel things. Because they’ve been sold artificial whatever on social media and screens. So they will love it or they will hate it. But they do it with such a passion.”

Critics notwithstanding, Refn seems in a content place right now. Is he actually glad his heart packed in? “I’m so happy, I can’t tell you,” he says. “Every day I thank God for killing me and bringing me back. Because why make me go through all this if I don’t have a purpose? Now I have a mission.”

If he gets another 25 years, he says, he will use them to make art, to forge new films from the furnace of his roaring creative fire. After all, he says, there’s nothing else out there. “There is no afterlife. I can say that. I didn’t see the light. So whatever time you have left, live it now, man.”

What about all the people who’ve had near-death experiences and claim to have seen the heavenly gates? Refn sniffs and, with no visible irony, says: “They’ve seen too many movies.”

Her Private Hell is in cinemas on 25 September
